Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents

Runhan Huang    Xiangcheng Zhang    Haoyu Chen    Yitong Li    Yen-Jen Wang    Bohan Lyu    Haotian Ye    Chuye Hong    Yixuan Wang    Chloe Su    Haoyu Xiong    Yangzhen Wu    Enze Xie    Travis Manderson    Stefano Ermon    Pieter Abbeel    Antonio Torralba    Dawn Song    Weirui Ye    Yilun Du Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Robot learning has advanced significantly by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. Furthermore, resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code directly, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop for fast inference. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across fine-grained precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4%+37.4\% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent system capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot agent collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform that allows new robot embodiments to be integrated solely via API interfaces, bypassing teleoperated data collection and policy training entirely. More details are available on our project page at robot-agent-exploration.com.

1 Introduction

  • “We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered. Building in our discoveries only makes it harder to see how the discovering process can be done.”

    — Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson (2019)

Robot learning has made substantial progress by scaling demonstration data and model capacity with imitation learning, aiming to replicate the training recipe that transformed language modeling (Kaplan et al., 2020). Vision-language-action (VLA) models and World-Action models (WAMs) fine-tune pretrained VLMs and video generation models, respectively, using large teleoperation corpora (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024). However, deploying a new robot or task still requires a dedicated teleoperation corpus of its own (O’Neill et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026e; Yuan et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Bi et al., 2026). Furthermore, the knowledge of such policy models is inherently bounded by the demonstrations they imitate. Consider a mobile robot tasked with loading a car in an unfamiliar house: while opening doors, grasping bags, and placing objects may each be familiar skills, the robot must adapt to novel scenes, visual appearances, and task compositions while discovering new approaches. This adaptation and discovery process is absent during imitation learning on static teleoperation data. Consequently, these policies struggle to generalize and self-improve, even when provided with environment interactions and test-time compute. This limitation motivates a central question: can robots self-improve and learn to discover new skills through autonomous online experience and active exploration?

Humans learn physical skills by attempting a task, observing the outcome, diagnosing failures, and practicing until their behavior becomes reliable. LLM agents exhibit a similar pattern in software domains: they explore unfamiliar systems by executing programs, inspecting outputs, and revising their work (Yang et al., 2024). Instead of training policies exclusively on teleoperated demonstration data, we let agents program robots directly (Lozano-Perez, 1983) without hand-designed action primitives. The agent explores online to discover decisions that drive task success, then automates these decision-making principles into modular robot programs that integrate perception, planning, and control. It continuously debugs and tests these programs through online execution. These programs encode the agent’s underlying principles for how to generate successful actions based on environment perception, rather than merely mimicking the actions themselves, thereby enabling more robust generalization. Furthermore, the agent can compose, modify, and update these programs when confronting increasingly complex scenes and tasks, continually improving through online experience.

We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), a cognitive architecture for robot agents. Its core organizing principle is scaling exploration: robot agents should improve by gathering their own online experience and optimizing their programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent receives a natural-language instruction, at most a few goal images or visual demonstrations, and a budget of exploration episodes. It interacts directly through the robot’s perception and control interfaces without requiring human teleoperation or value function guidance. The underlying language model parameters remain fixed and no policies are trained; instead, learning updates a persistent workspace of programs, notes, and verified skills. The agent converts successful interactions into autonomous code programs and stores reusable knowledge for subsequent episodes and tasks.

As exploration scales, we observe several emergent system capabilities: the agent constructs task-relevant 3D perception models, plans actions via pose search in 3D joint space, generates fully automated programs with closed-loop visual and force feedback, and adapts its programs when encountering novel task conditions. Furthermore, we observe agentic behaviors on real robots, including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and active human-robot interaction. For example, the robot executes end-effector contact probing for precise localization when depth measurements are inaccurate. In mobile manipulation experiments, following an initial collision with a cabinet, the agent automatically instantiates a safety check to verify workspace clearance before every base rotation. To test code robustness, the agent actively requests the human operator to vary object layouts, systematically testing the spatial generalization of the autonomous program.

In RAX, we equip the agent with rich multimodal sensing by exposing metric depth and force signals through the robot interface. A unified architecture supports tabletop bimanual arms, dexterous hands, mobile household robots, and humanoids through interfaces to each robot’s sensors, controllers, and kinematic models (Section 4). Unlike standard VLAs or WAMs operating on RGB images alone, the agent autonomously leverages these rich sensing signals to construct 3D point clouds and fit object models directly from perception. It then searches for actions to manipulate these 3D models while accounting for their unique shapes and affordances. Force feedback further enables the agent to resolve spatial uncertainty through contact and enable close-loop control on force signals in insertion tasks. Such multimodal world modeling have been largely absent from generalist policy models, yet naturally align with human cognitive processes.

To enable high-frequency closed-loop control, the agent compiles its decision-making process into executable Python programs that generate actions directly from sensor signals. Unlike prior approaches that rely on human-designed action primitives or policies trained on demonstrations (Lu et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026), our approach directly generates robot control programs that encapsulate the full perception-planning-control loop, whereas standard policies discard the underlying decision-making process essential for generalization. In practice, we observe the agent writing programs that automatically segment and identify objects in 3D using point-cloud fitting and hue-based identification, then plan actions grounded in this 3D world model, with retry loops and exception handling naturally incorporated into the code. Because actions are planned directly on perceived 3D objects rather than learned through imitation, this approach generalizes to far more diverse object layouts and domain variations than standard VLAs or WAMs. For semantically rich perception in open-world environments, the agent can program direct API calls to LLMs (such as Gemini) within the code to assist with object identification, while incorporating checkpoints and exception handling to step in and verify progress. Over the course of exploration, both action inference latency and token counts decrease as an increasing fraction of decisions becomes automated through code.

As experience scales with exploration, RAX maintains an intra-task memory file system across episodes to record failure lessons and successful strategies, allowing the agent to continually refine its programs. Across multiple tasks and sessions, we maintain a repository of modular programs as verified skills for various tasks and manipulation primitives. Each skill includes the executable code for a specific task, accompanied by execution logs from successful runs, clear preconditions, and verification checkpoints, allowing skills to be composed and reused for complex downstream tasks. In real-world mobile manipulation experiments in household settings, the agent practices individual tasks, each in its own exploration session, such as picking and placing boxes or tucking in office chairs, and commits them as verified skills. When subsequently evaluated on a composite, long-horizon task involving more than six sequential object manipulations, the agent achieves substantial automation and efficiency gains by reusing these stored skills. We envision agents practicing skills in a distributed, parallel fashion to build a rich repository of diverse capabilities, thereby enabling continual lifelong learning.

Using RAX, we conduct the first large-scale, multi-embodiment, systematic study of scaling exploration for robot agents, spanning fine-grained precision and long-horizon tasks across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboDojo, DexJoCo, BEHAVIOR-1K, and HumanoidArena in simulation and on two real robots. We evaluate the resulting policies on unseen scenes, separating exploration from evaluation. Performance grows steadily with exploration, and on fine-grained and long-horizon tasks on which state-of-the-art methods rarely succeed, RAX achieves high success rates, surpassing the strongest prior models by +37.4 on average over five benchmarks (1, Section 13). Without any expert action trajectories, RAX sets a new state of the art on RoboDojo (+53.4), BEHAVIOR-1K (+38.3), DexJoCo (+31.4), and LIBERO-Pro (+21.2). On HumanoidArena, it sets a new state of the art (+7.9) with three teleoperated demonstrations per task, where every baseline uses 100. On real Franka and Rainbow RB-Y1 robots, RAX masters five complex tabletop manipulation tasks and a long-horizon mobile manipulation task with zero demonstrations, and verified skills accumulated across sessions let later sessions build on earlier ones.

We summarize our contributions below:

  1. 1.

    We introduce RAX and establish scaling online exploration as a foundational principle for agentic robotics. In RAX, the agent operates directly through perception and robot control interfaces without policy training, compiling successful decision sequences into executable code programs that run autonomous execution loops.

  2. 2.

    Using RAX, we conduct the first systematic, multi-embodiment study of scaling online exploration across simulation and real robot environments. RAX acquires diverse manipulation capabilities solely through autonomous exploration, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by +37.4+37.4 points on average across five simulation benchmarks, while solving high-precision, deformable, articulated, and long-horizon manipulation tasks on real robots without human demonstrations.

  3. 3.

    We demonstrate rapid adaptation and continual learning on real robots, showing that generated programs can be selectively updated in response to environmental and task shifts while retaining verified skills in a persistent repository for composition and reuse in complex tasks.

We release the full architecture of RAX, together with its agent instructions, skills, benchmark integrations, and evaluation protocols, as a generalist robot-agent platform, on which a new robot can be brought up through an interface alone, without data collection or policy training.

2 Related Work

Language Models for Robot Control.

A substantial body of work uses pretrained language models as high-level planners or program generators for robots. SayCan grounds language-model plans in learned affordances (Ahn et al., 2022), Inner Monologue folds environment feedback into iterative replanning (Huang et al., 2022), and Code as Policies, ProgPrompt, and VoxPoser synthesize executable programs, situated task plans, or 3D value maps directly from instructions (Liang et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023). These methods typically invoke the model zero-shot or with a few in-context examples, producing a plan or a program that is executed with little opportunity to improve from experience. RAX instead treats the language model as a learner: it interacts with the robot over many episodes and revises its perception and control programs according to what it observes.

Agentic Robot Learning.

More recently, several works let coding agents improve robot behavior through interaction. ENPIRE runs agents in a closed loop of automatic reset, rollout, and policy training on a fleet of bimanual arms, and accelerates discovery by scaling the fleet (Xiao et al., 2026); FAEA and Encore refine policy programs from execution feedback, the latter starting from a few teleoperated demonstrations (Tsui et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026); Baton explores long-horizon tasks subtask by subtask with transition-aware memory (Xu et al., 2026); SimEX develops robot skills in a simulator reconstructed from the physical workspace before a few trials on the real robot (Hu et al., 2026); RPG practices in simulation on tasks derived from an offline trajectory dataset and refines a library of reusable skills (Wang et al., 2026d); EmbodiedSWE turns coding-agent solutions into training data for vision-language-action models (You et al., 2026); and CaP-X benchmarks coding agents on manipulation (Fu et al., 2026). These works establish that agents can improve robot behavior through interaction, and have so far demonstrated it mainly in tabletop manipulation with parallel-jaw grippers (Xiao et al., 2026; Tsui et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d), often on a single platform (Xiao et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d), with humanoid and mobile settings explored through pretrained locomotion (You et al., 2026) or short pick-up tasks (Fu et al., 2026). Several also draw on demonstrations (Kang et al., 2026), offline datasets (Wang et al., 2026d), reconstructed simulators (Hu et al., 2026), or neural policy training (Xiao et al., 2026). RAX complements these efforts: it learns each task on the robot itself, from its own exploration, and does so across single-arm and bimanual manipulators, dexterous hands, mobile manipulators performing long-horizon household activities, and legged humanoids whose locomotion the agent constructs itself, on established benchmarks and on real robots. On this basis, it studies systematically how performance scales with exploration, with 3D perception, and with accumulated memory.

Scaling Robot Learning.

Vision-language-action models (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024) and imitation learning methods (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2025) improve robot capability by scaling demonstration data and model size, and world action models extend this recipe by learning to predict how the scene evolves together with the actions that produce it (Wang et al., 2026e; Yuan et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Bi et al., 2026). To cover multiple embodiments, generalist policies pool demonstrations across robots into a single training mixture (O’Neill et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024; Doshi et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025), and a robot outside this mixture requires data of its own and further fine-tuning. In language modeling, computation spent at inference has emerged as a further scaling axis (Guo et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2024). RAX instead studies how robot capability grows with online experience acquired and organized by the agent itself, without additional demonstrations or parameter updates. Because this experience is gathered on the robot at hand, RAX extends to a new embodiment without pooled data, and adapts to it within a few episodes of exploration.

Memory and Cognitive Architectures.

Language agents can retain experience as explicit memory: Voyager grows a library of code skills through open-ended exploration in a game (Wang et al., 2023), and Reflexion and ExpeL distill feedback into textual lessons that improve later attempts (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024). At a broader level, classical cognitive architectures such as Soar and ACT-R structure intelligent behavior around perception, memory, and deliberation (Laird et al., 1987; Anderson et al., 2004), CoALA revisits this structure for language agents (Sumers et al., 2023), and Sutton’s common model of the intelligent agent (Sutton, 2022) and OaK architecture (Sutton et al., 2022) hold that all task-specific knowledge should be acquired at runtime from the agent’s own experience, a view developed further as the era of experience (Silver and Sutton, ). RAX brings this view to physical robots, where every skill is executable control code that enters memory only after it succeeds without supervision.

3 The RAX Cognitive Architecture

Inspired by Sutton’s OaK architecture (Sutton et al., 2022), RAX acquires all task-specific knowledge at runtime from the agent’s own experience. Building on task-agnostic robot control interfaces and low-level controllers, the agent autonomously develops task-specific perception, manipulation strategies, and executable skills through exploration. The following modules surround the language-model core: perception and control, autonomous robot program, and memory for continual learning (Figure 2).

3.1 Multimodal Perception

To build a physically accurate model of the world, we equip the agent with multimodal sensory inputs, including RGB images, depth maps, camera parameters, and force signals. The agent can thus construct 3D world models using depth data while regulating contact via force feedback. Notably, the 3D perception and object model fitting behaviors completely emerges from the agent exploration process, while we provide no skills, instructions or examples regarding specific usage of these multimodal sensing signals.

A real-robot task illustrates this process: opening an air fryer’s drawer, placing a banana in its basket, and closing the drawer (Figure 3). The agent lifts RGB-D observations into a point cloud in the robot’s base frame and constructs a geometric model of the fryer from its own measurements, localizing it in each new scene layout by fitting the fryer’s axis and handle direction with robust estimators. Because the drawer moves, the model is articulated, consisting of a fixed body and a drawer that slides along a prismatic joint. The agent plans every action, including grasping, pulling, and releasing, on this model and checks each motion for collisions. Section 14.2.1 details the model, the estimators, and how the program uses them. On a humanoid, the same process yields a gravity-aligned frame from the floor plane, landmarks for self-localization, and tracking updates after every gait cycle.

3.2 Planning and Control

Given the accurate world model, the agent then directly plans the robot actions in 3D world using robot control SDK and kinematic solvers. As the interface between the agent and the physical robot, we expose the robot’s control SDK as MCP tools, together with helpers such as an inverse kinematics (IK) solver and the robot’s URDF model. With these tools, the agent plans each motion and searches for feasible trajectories, accounting for the robot’s posture, collisions, and joint limits. In the air fryer task (Section 14.2), the drawer’s handle has a short horizontal arm on top and a grip hanging down from its end. Grasping the grip from the front, as a person would, leaves the arm almost no joint margin near its base for the pull, so the agent grasps the short arm from above and pulls the drawer open in 3 cm steps (actions 1 and 2 in Figure 3(b)). The 18 cm banana barely fits the 19 cm basket: released from a level hand, it touched the top of the fryer, and the opening fingers would hit the fryer’s body. The agent therefore tilts the hand by 60∘60^{\circ} about the banana’s axis, with the banana’s concave side toward the fryer, and releases it with its middle just beyond the basket’s center (action 3). The agent found these motions itself, by searching through the control tools during exploration, without human advice or demonstrations; Figure 27 shows them on the real robot.

3.3 From Exploration to Autonomous Robot Program

Generating each action with LLM-reasoning is expensive and slow. To enable high-frequency close-loop planning, the agent automates the decision process into a autonomous robot program with code that can directly execute to complete the task. Unlike prior work on coding agents for robotics (Lu et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026), we do not rely on hand-designed primitive skills or train policies by imitating human demonstrations, which inherently restricts scaling beyond human capability (Sutton, 2019). Instead, RAX agents directly control the robot without pre-trained policies or hand-coded primitives, progressively transferring control from high-level deliberation to autonomous code programs, resulting in autonomous decision-making through agent-native coding. Initially, the agent controls the robot through tool calls while perceiving the scene via the core LLM. Upon achieving task success, it compiles these decisions into code programs that run independently of main-agent deliberation. For example, after identifying object shapes and geometries, the agent generates a 3D object model and automatically estimates its position and pose using depth-derived point clouds when encountering new layouts. This eliminates the need for the main agent to repeatedly perceive and process raw images, which is slow and costly.

The agent decomposes tasks into stages and implements modular skills with programs that check preconditions, execute motions, and verify outcomes, operating much like a software development process through testing, debugging, and code versioning. Empirical measurements from exploration, such as gait-cycle distance or reliable grasp orientation, become program parameters. The agent tests successive code versions during exploration and uses stage-level failures to identify which specific skill requires revision. The hammer-delivery program on the HumanoidArena DoubleDesk task (Section 11.3), for instance, decouples approach, grasp, transit, obstacle crossing, and placement so that every failure traces directly to a specific stage (Figure 20).

Once reliable, the program is tested unattended in a new scene with exception handling and agent monitoring the generated logs in case of emergency situations. If perception or planning fails due to significant open-world variations, the program throws an exception, enabling the agent to step in, perceive the environment, and make necessary adjustments. Through scaled program testing and debugging during exploration, the result is a fully automated program that perceives, decides, and acts in unseen scenes with minimal or no agent intervention. Automated perception and planning allow it to adapt to new layouts in ways that replayed trajectories cannot. Deployment thus spans a continuum from the agent acting alone to a fully automated program, along which the agent advances as it accumulates experience.

3.4 Continual Learning with Memory

As online experience scales and decision-making becomes automated, RAX continually expands its capabilities by constructing persistent memory systems for reuse across episodes and tasks. Persistent memory carries experience at multiple timescales (Figure 2, top). Within a session, notes retain the current strategy, confirmed results, failed approaches, and useful parameters through context compression, which lives in the agent scratch pad in workspace. Across sessions and tasks, a skill repository stores each skill with its code, the conditions under which it applies, and evidence of its execution. It is continually contributed and merged by agents across different sessions and tasks, evolving with more experience.

A skill enters the repository only after it executes successfully without supervision, together with the evidence of that execution. Later sessions retrieve and compose skills that are known to work instead of rediscovering the same behavior. The benefit is largest on real robots, where every episode costs operator time: a grasp or a drawer-opening skill becomes a building block for longer tasks, and each session leaves the library more capable than it found it.

Learning via Practice

Much like humans, who repeatedly practice individual skills to gain proficiency before rehearsing complex, long-horizon tasks end-to-end, robot agents follow a similar cognitive progression. Here we depart from the conventional per-task training and evaluation protocol in robotics and frame robot learning as a continual process, where it generates and refines skills through practice and gradually moves on to more complex tasks by reusing the skills in the repository. Taking household tasks as an example, we let the agent practice individual subtasks, such as picking and placing (PnP) boxes and buckets or sorting tabletop items; each practice session is an exploration session on a single sub-task. During this process, the agent develops autonomous programs, rehearses them end-to-end to improve robustness, and eventually commits them to a multi-task skill library. During deployment on long-horizon compositional tasks, the agent reuses these subtask skills directly while verifying execution evidence and preconditions to handle environmental variations beyond those encountered during practice. Such skill acquisition and practice can also occur in parallel across multiple robots and tasks, enabling collective learning across multi-robot systems.

3.5 Parallel Multi-Agent and Multi-Environment Exploration

Online exploration can be time-consuming due to the latency of agent reasoning and environment execution. To accelerate this process, we parallelize exploration across multiple agents and environments, enabling agents to evaluate distinct strategies concurrently rather than sequentially within a single environment. In our simulation experiments, leveraging parallel environments and agents reduces the wall-clock time required to reach target performance by more than 2×2\times, highlighting the scalability of parallelized exploration for robotic systems. Section 5.3.1 measures how parallel exploration changes the time to consume the exploration budget and the score of the resulting program.

4 The RAX System

RAX supports a wide range of embodiments in simulation and in the real world, including single-arm and bimanual manipulators, dexterous hands, mobile manipulators, and humanoids, with one agent architecture. To do so, it adopts a separation familiar from software engineering, in which a frontend is kept apart from the backend that serves it. In RAX, the backend is the robot’s physical stack: the hardware drivers or the simulator, the low-level controllers, the sensor pipelines, and the safeguards around them. The frontend is the agent’s workspace, where the agent observes, decides, and acts, and where it writes the programs that encode its decision logic. The two meet only at a tool interface (Figure 4), and the same frontend connects to the backend of every platform, from the real Franka and Rainbow RB-Y1 robots to each simulated benchmark. The agent never touches the backend: it cannot modify controllers, drivers, or robot infrastructure. Because the agent acts only through these tools, its programs contain the decision logic of a task, namely perception, planning, and the checks between stages, while low-level control, from joint-level PD control to whole-body motion tracking on humanoids, and the enforcement of safety limits remain in the backend. The remainder of this section describes the separation and what each side provides (Section 4.1), and the control interface through which one frontend drives arms, dexterous hands, mobile manipulators, and humanoids (Section 4.2).

4.1 Frontend–Backend Separation

On a real robot, the backend owns everything that keeps the hardware calibrated and safe. It runs the vendor’s drivers and real-time controllers, serves calibrated RGB-D images together with the intrinsics and poses of their cameras, and records the robot’s sensors and state continuously, so that the agent can review the outcome of an action after the fact. It also enforces the safeguards. Motion is enabled only while an operator has armed the robot, and disarming halts it immediately; every motion command is validated before execution against workspace bounds, joint limits, and self-collision, and on the RB-Y1 mobile manipulator also against joint load. A command that violates a limit is refused before the robot moves, together with the limit it violated, so that the agent can change its approach.

The frontend receives exactly two things from the system, tools and skills. The tools expose as much of the backend as possible: observation, raw control, and model-based helpers in the form of forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning where the platform offers it, and a preview that executes a candidate motion on the robot model alone, without the scene. They also provide the geometric primitives on which perception is built, namely the back-projection of pixels to metric 3D points, the poses of the cameras in the robot’s frame, and the kinematic chain from each camera to the end-effectors. The skills are documents that describe how to work with these tools: the robot’s frames, action spaces, rates, limits, and failure modes, the conventions of perception, and the workflow of exploration and memory. They are organized along four axes, namely task strategy, coordination, perception, and robot-specific control, and are composed into a single workspace for each session according to its embodiment and observation mode. Everything that solves a task, from object models and perception pipelines to grasps and control code, is written by the agent, which works in an isolated container with a persistent workspace and standard programming tools.

This division has three consequences. First, programs written by the agent call exactly the tools that the agent itself calls, so code developed interactively runs unchanged as a fully automated program. Second, the interface returns compact results, consisting of structured state and the final image of each motion, while the complete images and actions of every motion are stored as episodic evidence that the agent retrieves on demand, which keeps the agent’s context small over sessions that last many hours. Third, on real robots, the skills that agents verify are kept in a versioned repository for each robot, in which every session works on its own branch, and a contribution is merged only after its structure, its entry point, and the evidence of its unattended success have been validated.

Most importantly, the separation makes RAX multi-embodiment by construction. Bringing up a new robot requires only a backend that exposes it through the tool interface, together with documentation of its control and sensing interfaces, while the frontend, the organization of memory, and the evaluation protocol are shared across all platforms. No expert teleoperation data is collected and no policy is trained to bring a robot into RAX. The single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid embodiments of our experiments, in simulation and in the real world, differ only in their backends and in the documentation of their interfaces, and the agent learns to control each of them through exploration.

4.2 Multi-Embodiment Control Interface

RAX adopts a layered control design. Low-level controllers, from joint position and impedance controllers to whole-body motion trackers, run in the backend and are responsible for high-rate tracking and stability, while the agent makes decisions at the level of short action chunks and motion goals. Each platform exposes raw control for full expressiveness, together with model-based helpers in the form of forward and inverse kinematics, collision-aware motion planning (Sundaralingam et al., 2023), and a robot-only preview that executes a candidate motion on the robot model without the scene. The agent thus chooses its own level of abstraction, from individual joint targets to planned free-space motions. Table 1 summarizes this construction for each platform.

On the real robots, the backend wraps each vendor’s own control stack. The Franka FR3 arm runs joint impedance control, and the agent commands straight-line Cartesian moves of the tool center point, joint-space moves whose paths are checked against the workspace and the table before the arm moves, and force-controlled grasps that close the gripper to a target width with a set force. The Rainbow RB-Y1, a wheeled mobile manipulator with a torso, two arms, and a two-joint head that carries an RGB-D camera, runs joint position control on its robot controller, which also accepts Cartesian IK commands for the torso and arms. The agent commands end-effector poses, joint-space postures of the torso, arms, and head, coordinated motions of the torso and arms, motions of the differential-drive base, and the gaze of the head camera. It can query the vendor’s kinematic model for the collisions, joint load, and center of mass of any posture, and dry-run any motion command to learn whether it would be accepted. Neither robot offers a motion planner, so the agent composes long motions from short checked moves through clear intermediate postures.

On the HumanoidArena benchmark (Wang et al., 2026b), the agent commands the Unitree G1 through whole-body kinematic references rather than joint torques: each reference specifies a desired heading, a full joint configuration, and hand commands, and a whole-body motion tracker converts these references into balanced whole-body motion. Because the robot moves through space only by stepping, locomotion is not provided as a primitive but must be constructed by the agent from leg references, and agents do so by measuring their own gait, calibrating step length, and composing walking, turning, and stepping over obstacles from these measurements.

On DexJoCo (Wang et al., 2026a), the official operational-space controller tracks the flange pose of each arm while position actuators drive the sixteen joints of each Allegro hand, and no motion planner is provided, so the agent plans the motion of each arm and the configuration of each hand itself. The remaining simulated platforms span the same range of abstraction. The single arm of LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro (Liu et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2025) is driven through the benchmark’s own operational-space controller by relative end-effector commands alone, whereas on RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026a) and BEHAVIOR-1K (Li et al., 2023) the native controllers execute joint targets under each benchmark’s own dynamics, and inverse kinematics and motion planning are offered as helpers alongside raw control rather than as replacements for it. Motion planning accounts for the robot and static structures but never for task objects, which the agent must perceive itself.

5 Experiments

In this section we report our simulation benchmark results as well as case studies on both simulation and real robot experiments.

5.1 Setup

We comprehensively evaluate RAX in both simulated environments and on real-world robotic hardware. In simulation, the evaluation spans six benchmarks covering single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid embodiments: RoboDojo, BEHAVIOR-1K, HumanoidArena, DexJoCo, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Pro. In each session, a coding agent starts in a localized workspace containing only the platform’s baseline skills. Guided by a task description and RGB-D observations, the agent explores training scenes within a strictly defined episode budget. The submitted code is then executed as a fully automated program under each benchmark’s official evaluation protocol (Section 10).

On physical robots, RAX is deployed on a Franka FR3 manipulator to master five distinct tabletop tasks: (1) memory, tracking and finding a hidden cube randomly shuffled under four cups (Section 14.1); (2) articulated objects, opening an air fryer drawer, inserting a banana, and closing it (Section 14.2); (3) deformable objects, wiping a stain off a table using a wet towel (Section 14.3); (4) precision, inserting pegs into a ManipulationNet board with a stringent 0.1,mm clearance (Section 14.4); and (5) precision and long horizon, dismantling and rebuilding a Bandu tower of irregular pieces (Section 14.5).

Additionally, we evaluate RAX on a Rainbow RB-Y1 mobile manipulator to solve a long-horizon logistical task. This involves pulling out a chair, stacking cups, picking up a banana, loading the items into a basket, carrying the basket to a cabinet, tucking the chair back, and subsequently transferring a box to the cabinet (Section 14.6). Crucially, the agent receives only natural-language instructions and zero teleoperated demonstrations. It is designed to autonomously evaluate its own success criteria, only prompting a human operator to reset the physical scene between trials.

5.2 Simulation Results

Here we report the simulation benchmark results across RoboDojo, BEHAVIOR-1K, HumanoidArena, DexJoCo, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Pro.

5.2.1 RoboDojo

Setup.

We measure exploration scaling on seven RoboDojo tasks with the dual-arm ARX X5 (Section 10.3), spanning domain-randomized variants (make toast random, hang mugs random, sweep blocks random), as well as precision (plug in charger), memory (swap blocks), long-horizon (make kong), and open-instruction (pour by language) tasks. For each task, a single agent explores a single environment from an empty workspace, given the task’s public scoring rubric with a short clarification of its conditions, RGB-D observations, and one image of the task’s completed state. Sessions differ only in the exploration budget NN (i.e., the number of exploration episodes), with each episode conducted in a new exploration scene. At the end of exploration, the agent submits its rehearsed bundle. The resulting fully automated program is then evaluated without the agent on 30 to 50 unseen scenes, scored by the native evaluator with partial credit.

Baselines.

We compare our approach with the five strongest learned policies on the RoboDojo-Sim leaderboard (Chen et al., 2026a), which are trained on demonstrations, and with PhysicalRSI, an agent-based system listed separately on the same leaderboard (Table 2).

Results.

With its largest budget on each task, RAX exceeds every baseline on all seven tasks, averaging 78.3% compared to 24.9% for VPP2, the strongest policy on the leaderboard (Table 2). The margins are largest where learned policies make little progress: on sweep blocks random, RAX reaches 71.7% where the best baseline achieves only 8.0%; and on pour by language, which every learned policy fails, it reaches 100.0%. Performance consistently grows with the exploration budget. Plug in charger rises from 26.0% with 4 exploration episodes to 94.0% with 8; swap blocks improves from 34.0% to 100.0% with 16; and make kong—for which the agent submitted no program within 8 episodes—increases from 64.0% with 16 episodes to 96.0% with 32. The domain-randomized tasks require the largest budgets: make toast random rises from 2.5% with 16 episodes to 31.7% with 32 and 47.2% with 64, and sweep blocks random improves from 53.3% to 71.7%, while hang mugs random stays between 33.3% and 39.2% across all budgets.

5.2.2 BEHAVIOR-1K

Setup.

We evaluate RAX on six long-horizon household tasks from the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge (Li et al., 2023), where previous challenge entries have struggled to make progress. For each task, cooperating agents explore parallel environments using the Galaxea R1Pro for 128 exploration episodes, given the task description, RGB-D observations, and an image sequence of a successful completion (keyframes of official demonstrations, without actions or states). We evaluate the agent-in-the-loop program: a fresh copy of the agent starts from the frozen workspace and attempts each of the ten public test instances of the challenge—the same instances used to report public results.

Review reports.

Throughout exploration, after each run of the agent’s code, a separate review model provides detailed feedback to the agent regarding the outcome. This report outlines any missed goal conditions and their likely causes, suggests the most valuable code changes, and includes the run’s partial score alongside key camera frames (Section 10.4).

Scoring and baselines.

Episodes are evaluated using the challenge’s Q-score, which measures the fraction of satisfied goal conditions and awards full credit for a complete success. We compare our approach against the five highest-ranked entries from the challenge (Table 3). Figure 6 illustrates the program RAX generates for the boxing books task.

5.2.3 HumanoidArena

Setup.

We evaluate RAX on all seven tasks of HumanoidArena (Wang et al., 2026b) that have official test episodes: three human–object interaction tasks (Football, DoubleDesk, and P&PBox) and four human–scene interaction tasks (OpenDoor, SitSofa, Boxing, and VisNavi), on a Unitree G1 with Dex3 hands (Section 10.5). The agent commands whole-body reference poses, which the SONIC motion tracker (Luo et al., 2026) turns into balanced whole-body motion. The agent perceives the scene through the egocentric RGB-D camera and receives the task description together with three teleoperated demonstrations, which are available only to the exploring agent. It explores with a budget of up to 128 episodes on DoubleDesk and P&PBox and up to 32 episodes on each of the other tasks, on scenes drawn from the training distribution and never on a test episode, and the resulting fully automated program is evaluated alone, without the agent, on unseen scenes, the 60 official test episodes of each task.

Baselines.

We compare with the baselines of the benchmark, ACT (Zhao et al., 2023), Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2025), a flow-matching policy (Boston Dynamics and Toyota Research Institute, 2025), and the VLA π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025), each trained on 100 teleoperated demonstrations per task, and with WB-WAM (Qin et al., 2026), a world action model pretrained on 1,880 hours of video and motion data and fine-tuned on the same 100 demonstrations per task, all with the same tracker (Table 4).

Results.

RAX reaches an average success rate of 89.8% (Table 4), 7.9 points above WB-WAM and 29.8 points above the strongest baseline of the benchmark, from three demonstrations instead of one hundred. It succeeds in every test episode of OpenDoor and Boxing, and on Football and VisNavi it improves on WB-WAM by 28.3 and 16.6 points. Performance grows with the exploration budget: averaged over the seven tasks, the success rate rises from 52.1% with 2 exploration episodes to 80.7% with 32. Tasks governed by whole-body posture and locomotion, such as OpenDoor and SitSofa, are solved within a few episodes, Football and VisNavi rise from 40.0% and 71.7% to 98.3% and 93.3%, and the two whole-body loco-manipulation tasks keep improving with further exploration, P&PBox from 0.0% to 83.3% and DoubleDesk from 0.0% to 56.7% at 128 episodes. We also test RAX with the three demonstrations without their actions (RAX ⋆, Section 5.3.4): without any action data, it still matches the 81.9% average of WB-WAM, which is fine-tuned on 100 action demonstrations per task.

5.2.4 DexJoCo

Setup.

DexJoCo (Wang et al., 2026a) evaluates task-oriented dexterous manipulation with Franka arms that carry 16-degree-of-freedom Allegro hands, on six single-arm and five bimanual tasks. The agent commands the end-effector pose of each arm and the joint positions of each hand. It perceives the scene through RGB-D observations and receives the task description and three completion images of expert episodes as a goal reference, but no action demonstrations or expert videos. For each task, a single agent explores a single environment from an empty workspace, with the exploration episodes drawn from the training distribution of the rand-obj setting and never on an evaluation layout. Sessions differ only in the exploration budget, from 2 to 32 exploration episodes, and the resulting fully automated program is evaluated alone, without the agent, on unseen scenes, the 150 official evaluation episodes of each task (Section 10.6).

Baselines.

We compare with the baselines of the benchmark, Diffusion Policy with transformer and CNN backbones (Chi et al., 2025), ACT (Zhao et al., 2023), and the VLAs π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025) and GR00T N1.5 (Bjorck et al., 2025), each trained on 100 teleoperated demonstrations per task, and with subsequent results on the same benchmark: GR00T N1.6, the world action models Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026), PointWAM (Park et al., 2026), which pretrains on 1.15 million human videos, and ME-Dex (Zhang et al., 2026), and the diffusion transformer DECO (Li et al., 2026) (Table 5).

Results.

Performance grows rapidly with exploration (Table 5): averaged over the eleven tasks, the success rate rises from 31.9% with 2 exploration episodes to 86.9% with 8 and 96.7% with 32, and with 32 exploration episodes RAX exceeds the best published result on every task. Hammer, Mouse, and iPad are solved from two exploration episodes, most other tasks within four to eight, and the bimanual Assembly within sixteen. Taking the best session of each task, RAX succeeds in every evaluation episode of eight of the eleven tasks and reaches an average success rate of 99.5%, 45.4 points above the strongest baseline of the benchmark and 34.2 points above the best published average, without a single action demonstration. The margins are largest on the bimanual tasks that existing methods rarely complete: RAX solves Hanoi (Section 11.2) and iPad in every episode, where the best published results are 42.0 and 52.0, and reaches 96.0 on Assembly, where the best published result is 28.0.

5.2.5 LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro

Setup.

LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) evaluates a single Franka Panda arm with a parallel-jaw gripper on four ten-task suites, Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long (Section 10.7), and LIBERO-Pro (Zhou et al., 2025) perturbs the layouts of the same tasks. The agent commands delta end-effector poses and the gripper. It perceives the scene through the agent-view and wrist RGB-D cameras and receives the task description and three images of the completed task, but no action demonstrations. It explores with a budget of up to 20 episodes on fresh layouts drawn from the official placement distribution and may continue with up to 5 episodes of adaptation on layouts drawn from the position-perturbed distribution of LIBERO-Pro, in which objects exchange their initial regions (Section 11.4), never on an evaluation state. The resulting fully automated program is evaluated alone, without the agent, on unseen scenes, the 50 official initial states of each task and the 50 position-perturbed states of LIBERO-Pro.

Baselines.

We compare with the VLAs OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024), OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025), π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2024), π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025), and X-VLA (Zheng et al., 2026), and with the world action models Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026), Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026), PatchWAM (Wang et al., 2026c), and VPP2 (Guo et al., 2026), all of which fine-tune on the benchmark’s demonstrations (Table 6).

Results.

Without a single action demonstration, RAX achieves one of the highest average success rates among these models on the original suites, 98.5% (Table 6). Under position perturbation the learned policies collapse: OpenVLA, π0\pi_{0}, and X-VLA succeed in at most 2% of the episodes of any suite, π0.5\pi_{0.5} in at most 38%, and the world action models PatchWAM and VPP2 in 8.8% and 42.3% on average. Without a single episode on perturbed layouts, the programs of RAX, which locate every object anew in each episode, already retain 76.0% on average and exceed every learned policy on every suite, 33.7 points above VPP2; they also exceed by 12.8 points the coding agent ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026), which develops a program for each task and perturbation with up to 75 rollouts and evolutionary search on instances from the evaluation distribution (Section 12). With at most 5 episodes of adaptation on perturbed layouts, RAX raises its average by a further 8.4 points to 84.4%, from 71.4% on Long to 100.0% on Object, and exceeds ASPIRE on every suite. Exploration thus yields programs that transfer to new layouts, and a few further episodes of exploration repair those that do not.

5.3 Ablations

In this section we ablate the key design choices of our system, including parallel exploration with multi-agent and multiple environments, the effect of depth sensing over RGB-only observations, and the evolve of inference tokens and inference time over exploration.

5.3.1 Parallelization

Exploration can also be parallelized (Section 3.5): the same budget of exploration episodes is distributed across KK parallel environments, explored by a team of cooperating agents that share a common workspace. In the same way that multiple agents scale test-time compute in parallel rather than purely serially, trading some efficiency for wall-clock time, parallel environments let a team of agents consume an exploration budget concurrently. We parallelize exploration on make toast. All sessions use RGB-D observations, an image sequence of one successful completion, and instructions that summarize the official task code, including its numeric success thresholds; the fully automated program is evaluated on the same 32 unseen scenes. Parallelization reduces the time needed to consume the exploration budget for both agents (Table 7). With four agents in four environments, Claude Code reaches a score of 92.2 in 4.9 hours, against 63.3 in 13.7 hours for a single agent with a larger budget; with two agents in two environments, Codex matches its single-agent score in 9.2 hours instead of 14.2.

5.3.2 Depth versus RGB-Only Perception

To measure the contribution of depth, we compare RGB-D and RGB-only sessions on the three domain-randomized RoboDojo tasks. In the RGB-only profile, depth and the geometric primitives built on it are removed, and the agent must perceive through motion, relating image coordinates to robot motion by moving the robot by known amounts. Each pair shares the task, the agent, and the exploration budget NN, and its fully automated program is evaluated on the same unseen scenes as in Section 5.2.1. With depth, the agent outperforms the RGB-only agent in every pair, by 17.3 points on average (Table 8).

Case study: perception with and without depth.

To understand where this gap comes from, we inspect the fully automated programs submitted by the RGB-D and RGB-only agents on make toast random with a budget of 32 episodes. Both agents use the vision-language model in the same role, to point at semantic image locations such as the toaster slots, the top crust of a bread slice, and the lever. They differ in how they turn these image points into motion.

With depth. The RGB-D agent lifts every image point into a metric 3D point and builds the task’s geometry from these points. It first refines each slot opening by fitting a line to its visible contour, then measures both rim endpoints of each slot in 3D, from which it derives the slot centers and their common heading. On the bread, it measures two points along the top crust and one on the near side, and recovers the slice’s full 3D orientation from the plane through these points. After the grasp, it measures the slice again in the wrist camera to obtain its pose in the hand, and repeats this measurement above the slot to correct any slip before release. The agent also uses metric geometry to verify its perception: a measurement is rejected when a rim point does not lie within a narrow band at the toaster’s roof height, when the two rim endpoints are not 9 to 20 cm apart, or when the two slots are not 2.6 to 7.5 cm apart, and a press of the lever counts only when the lever is measured to have travelled 2.5 to 13 cm downward.

Without depth. The RGB-only agent does not give up on 3D reasoning; it reconstructs a coarse camera model of its own. It maps overhead-camera pixels to table coordinates through a linear calibration at an assumed height, about 1.8 mm per pixel across the image and 1.4 mm per pixel along it, and then refines every target by visual servoing in the wrist camera: it moves the gripper until the target is centered, with hand-tuned gains of 0.4 to 0.8 mm per pixel, and rotates it until the slot or the bread is aligned in the image. The quantities that depth would provide are replaced by constants, including the grasp and release heights, the 3.8 cm spacing between the slots, and the height to which the lever is pressed, and success is judged by asking the vision-language model whether a slice is held or seated. These approximations hold only where the scene matches the agent’s assumptions. In evaluation, 36 of its 45 episodes ended in the lever stage without success, the step at which a fixed press height replaces a measured one, against 8 successes for the RGB-D agent.

5.3.3 Inference Time and Tokens

Here we demonstrate the decrease of inference wall time and output tokens with exploration as more and more decisions are being automated with programs.

Simulation

As the agent compiles its experience into autonomous code programs, the computational overhead of action generation decreases substantially. We evaluate this efficiency gain across two benchmark tasks: loading the car in BEHAVIOR-1K (128 exploration episodes across two parallel environments) and make toast random in RoboDojo (64 exploration episodes). We define episode inference time as the cumulative wall-clock latency dedicated to action generation—excluding simulator and hardware step times—regardless of whether actions stem from direct LLM deliberation, code program execution, or a hybrid mode. Figure 7 tracks inference latency and output token consumption across all successful exploration episodes. On loading the car, the initial successful episode required 123 minutes of inference time and 254k output tokens. By the final exploration episode, inference overhead dropped to 4 minutes and 4k tokens, while environment execution time remained over 1 hour per episode. Similarly, on make toast random, initial task completion required 17 minutes of inference latency. Once execution transitioned to the compiled program, inference latency for the final agent-monitored successes fell to 6 seconds per episode—matching the 3–7 seconds observed during standalone program rehearsals (which accounted for 7 of the 15 total successes).

Real robots

Similar efficiency trends hold on real robots using the Franka manipulator (Table 9). We evaluate air fryer manipulation (Section 14.2) and Bandu tower assembly (Section 14.5), comparing an initial trial in which the agent generates each action via active deliberation against a subsequent execution of the compiled autonomous program. In both paradigms, the system actuates the robot through identical tool interfaces, with robot time defined as the duration spent executing arm, gripper, and visual perception calls. For the air fryer task, initial task completion (including online exploration) required 72 minutes of inference latency and 262k output tokens, against 3 minutes of robot time. Upon compilation, the initial autonomous run required only 18 seconds of inference latency (attributable entirely to local programmatic execution), with four subsequent unattended trials consistently yielding latencies between 18 and 23 seconds. Similarly, on the Bandu tower, step-by-step LLM deliberation to assemble six blocks required 17 minutes of inference latency; once compiled, autonomous assembly of seven blocks completed with 10 seconds of program overhead alongside 11 minutes of continuous robot execution. During these autonomous runs, control proceeded without human intervention or online LLM action synthesis, while background monitoring generated at most 2.2k tokens per run in parallel without imposing latency on robot execution.

5.3.4 Demonstrations Without Actions

On HumanoidArena, the exploring agent reads three teleoperated demonstrations of each task, and its programs may reuse motion segments cut from them, such as a gait cycle (Section 11.3). We remove the actions from these demonstrations and keep everything else unchanged except the budget (RAX ⋆), which is 256 exploration episodes on DoubleDesk, 128 on P&PBox, and 64 on each of the other five tasks, and evaluate the program on the same 60 official test episodes. Without any action data, RAX ⋆ reaches 81.9% on average and matches WB-WAM, which is fine-tuned on 100 action demonstrations per task (Table 10). On Football, OpenDoor, and SitSofa, it stays within 5 points of RAX with action demonstrations. The more dynamic and contact-rich whole-body tasks, which require sustained locomotion or whole-body contact, VisNavi, Boxing, P&PBox, and DoubleDesk, remain 10.0 to 16.6 points lower despite larger budgets. When the agent has to discover a suitable gait and whole-body control on its own, whole-body loco-manipulation requires more exploration.

5.4 Intriguing Emerging Agentic Behaviors with Scaling Exploration

In this section, we analyze agentic behaviors that emerge as exploration scales, in simulation and on real robots; each task is detailed in Sections 11 and 14.

5.4.1 Active Perception

Active perception (Xiong et al., 2025) emerges naturally as the agent does not treat perception as a single look at the scene (Figure 8). It moves its cameras and its hand to obtain the measurements that a step needs, measures again before it acts, and checks the outcome of each action with a new measurement.

Simulation.

On the bimanual Tower of Hanoi of DexJoCo (Section 11.2), the agent received no model of its Allegro hands. It spent its first episode on its own hand: it moved single joints, lifted the wrist cameras’ depth into points to see what each joint moves, segmented the white fingertip caps, and fitted the fingertip offsets on which every grasp of its program is built; its thumb offset lies within 1.1 mm of the official model it never saw. On the LIBERO-Long task of putting two cans into a basket (Section 11.1), the program perceives the scene anew in every round; before each grasp, it hovers 7 cm above the can, refits the lid from the wrist camera, and rejects a top that is not can-shaped. Because the agent-view camera cannot see the floor of the basket, the program maps the basket from the wrist camera while it holds the first can, and maps it again after the first release. On the bimanual Tower of Hanoi of DexJoCo (Section 11.2), the program verifies every lift by measuring the held disk from three cameras and pinches again when the disk rose less than half of the lift; after placing the red disk, it measures the disk’s top again and finds it on average 0.66 mm below the height it predicted. On the humanoid that carries a hammer over a bar (Section 11.3), the program perceives anew at every stage and before every step at the bar, and it confirms a grasp by measuring the height of the handle again. Without depth, the RGB-only agent recovers metric relations by moving the robot by known amounts and servoing on the wrist camera (Section 5.3.2).

Real robot.

On the ManipulationNet peg-in-hole challenge (Chen et al., 2026b) (Section 14.4), the board is transparent acrylic, and the task text warned that the wrist camera’s depth is inaccurate at close range. The agent turned this warning into a measurement procedure that uses the arm itself as a probe: it closes the gripper, descends in 1.5 mm steps, and records the height at which the vertical force drops by 3 to 4 N. Touching the table at three points, it found that the table rises by about 3.4 mm per 10 cm along the robot’s xx axis and that the top of the board lies 24.7 mm above the table, against 25 mm in the board’s CAD model, and it models the height of the board’s top as a plane that rises along xx. Before each insertion into the row with 0.1 mm clearance, it touches the board next to the hole with the held peg, and these reference heights agree within 0.5 mm. Probing also calibrates the camera: from a hole whose centre it had located by touch, the agent found that the wrist camera’s absolute positions were offset by 6.4 and −0.8-0.8 mm, corrected every hole by this offset, and the next peg dropped into its hole on the first probe.

5.4.2 Error Recovery and Safety

On real robots, the agent’s mistakes have physical consequences, and it turns each one into a rule that its later programs follow (Figure 9). On the RB-Y1, an in-place turn that the agent planned by hand swung the rear of the base into a cabinet; from then on, the agent checked every base move against the area the base sweeps. Lifting a bucket while squatting overloaded a wrist and stopped the robot; standing up before the lift, a correction from the operator, resolved it, and the agent kept it as a rule in its skill. On the Franka, an unusual arm posture drove the elbow into a camera; the agent then restricted itself to natural arm postures, kept the arm away from the cameras, and recalibrated the bumped camera itself (Section 14.2.1). In simulation, the humanoid crosses a bar only from foot placements that its own falls showed to be safe (Section 11.3).

5.4.3 Human–Robot Interaction

The agent reaches the operator through a request tool and uses it with purpose (Figure 10). On the ManipulationNet board, after the board shifted during its attempts at tight fits, it asked the operator to tape the board to the table. On the air fryer (Section 14.2), it refused to pick a banana placed in front of the camera it had hit earlier, because its forearm would pass within about 1 cm of the camera, and asked for the banana to be moved. After unattended successes, it asked the operator to move and rotate the fryer, in effect designing its own tests of generalization: across runs 6 to 10, the fryer moved by up to 7 cm and its handle turned by up to 18∘, and the program succeeded unattended in every new placement but one, where it needed help and which exposed two errors in its program that the agent then fixed.

5.5 Continual Learning

In this section, we demonstrate how RAX achieves continual learning with robot programs: by reusing skills learned in earlier exploration sessions, and by rapidly adapting its programs when the environment or the task changes.

5.5.1 Reusing Skills

On the RB-Y1 mobile manipulator, RAX acquires skills through isolated exploration sessions and reuses them to solve long-horizon compositional tasks (Figure 11). In initial sessions, the agent independently learned to park and tuck an office chair, stack nested cups, transport a bucket by its rim onto a cabinet, and pick and place a box. Each skill was committed to the repository only after achieving successful end-to-end execution, stored as a versioned program bound to explicit precondition checks. The multi-stage tidy-up task (Figure 5) evaluates the composition of these skills under a single high-level goal: park the chair, stack the cups, place the cups and a banana inside the bucket, transport the bucket onto the cabinet, tuck the chair back under the desk, and finally pick the box onto the other empty cabinet.

Skills are called, not relearned

In the final execution of the tidy-up task, every stage is resolved by composing stored skills from the repository (Figure 11). The agent executes the chair skill sequentially: it estimates the chair geometry, plans a collision-free motion path, grasps the backrest, navigates along the path, and releases the target. It invokes the cup-stacking skill using semantic visual grounding from the current scene, applying fine-grained closed-loop offsets prior to insertion. For the bucket and box skills, the agent parameterizes execution using real-time perception data, such as the estimated cabinet boundary derived from depth sensing. To bridge gaps between stored skills, the agent dynamically synthesizes ad-hoc code—such as extending the grasp planner to handle a banana, commanding torso elevation prior to transit, and re-estimating desk pose before final chair insertion.

Skills are refined in use

Across three iterations of the tidy-up task, the agent iteratively updated program versions rather than rewriting entire control loops. The bucket and box skills required minor programmatic adjustments (∼\sim25 out of more than 1200 lines) to integrate dynamic cabinet-edge measurements from onboard depth perception. Skills encountering greater environmental domain shift underwent larger revisions: following two failed grasp attempts, the agent updated the chair skill to grasp 4 cm deeper, while extending the cup-stacking skill to support picking additional object classes.

Repository expansion

Intermediary control code synthesized by the agent to bridge task stages is modularized and saved as new skills. For instance, a synthesized hand-reach primitive was automatically abstracted, committed to the repository, and subsequently reused across both the chair-manipulation and cup-stacking routines.

5.5.2 Rapid Adaptation of Programs

When task conditions vary post-deployment, RAX preserves valid program subroutines and selectively updates only the modules invalidated by environmental shifts (Figure 12). On the Franka manipulator, two end-to-end autonomous programs were adapted to novel task variants within the same session.

Find the cube

In a hidden-object task, the physical occlusion sequence was modified: rather than directly inverting a cup over the target cube, the cube was placed inside an upright cup prior to inversion. The original program detected no covering cup and safely halted execution via exception handling without initiating ungrounded motion. The agent extended its perception pipeline with a detector for cubes contained within upright cups, validated the new logic against current and historical sensor logs, and resumed execution to complete the task (Figure 22). Crucially, the cup-tracking, execution-monitoring, and removal routines were reused without modification. When substituting the cube with a red wedge, the agent generalized its geometric object representation from a fixed cube primitive to an object parameterized by estimated dimensions, color, and height, adjusting grasp synthesis accordingly while preserving 20 of the original 41 program functions (including the tracking pipeline; Figure 23).

Wiping with paper towels

Following the acquisition of a reliable surface-wiping skill using a wet cloth, the task was extended to require pulling disposable paper towels from a dispenser box, executing the wiping motion, and discarding used towels into a receptacle. The agent synthesized a composite program that imported the original wiping module as a dependency. The new program reused existing subroutines for stain segmentation against the table background, reachable workspace estimation, pressing by position control (12​mm12\,\text{mm} below the measured surface contact, along a serpentine trajectory), and post-wipe residue verification. Only paper-handling subroutines were added: locating the dispenser box and disposal bin, extracting individual sheets onto the stain, discarding the crumpled towel, and clearing loose paper from the workspace. The stain was removed in both wet runs, although leftover sheets still had to be cleared with supervised scripts (Section 14.3, Figure 29).

6 Discussion

Progress in robot learning has largely been driven by collecting more demonstrations and training larger models. Our results show that a capable agent, when allowed to explore, continues to improve with the experience it accumulates, without teleoperation and without updates to its parameters. Because this form of learning relies on general-purpose agents whose capabilities are advancing rapidly in other domains, every improvement in those agents translates directly into improved robot learning.

The knowledge acquired by RAX agents takes the form of perception and control programs, skills, and notes. In this form, knowledge executes at the rate of the robot, can be inspected and verified, composes into longer behaviors, and transfers across tasks, and we expect code to play the same role for learning from experience that network parameters play for learning from data. Since the instructions, skills, and memory structures of RAX are themselves code and text, a natural next step is to let agents improve the architecture itself from experience, and to share verified skills across fleets of robots, so that a skill learned by one robot becomes available to all.
