8 Interface Contracts

On the real robots the agent acts only through tools that wrap each vendor’s control SDK, and its own programs call the same tools. Every command is checked before the robot moves; workspace, joint limit, or IK violations are refused, and motion works only while the operator has armed the robot. Table 11 summarizes the tools; both robots also offer status and request_operator.

9 Agent Instructions and Skills

Every session starts from the same workspace template: one instruction file and a folder of skills, written once and shared by all platforms (auto_research_agent/ and agent_skills/ in our code). Robot-specific facts, such as tool names, cameras, and control rates, are filled in when the workspace is built, so the agent reads the same instructions on every robot.

Instructions.

The instruction file fixes the order of work rather than how to solve any task. The agent first reads the task text and its own notes from earlier sessions, then (1) solves the task by controlling the robot directly through tools until it confirms success, (2) turns what it did into a program whose steps check their preconditions, verify their results, and report states they were not built for, (3) runs that program on every further exploration episode, stepping in where it falls short and fixing the code, and (4) keeps its notes, code, and a hand-off note current, since only those carry over to later sessions. In benchmark sessions it then freezes the program, rehearses it once end to end without help, and submits it. The file also states the budget rules: new layouts in every episode, so scene geometry is measured again rather than assumed, and a blocker is reported rather than bypassed.

Skills.

Skills are short documents that the agent opens when it reaches the step they cover. They are grouped by axis, task strategy, coordination, perception, and robot control, and a session receives only the layers that match its robot and observation mode. The task and coordination skills are robot-agnostic (Table 12); the perception and control layers give each robot’s interface under the same names, so a task skill can point to, for example, the robot’s interface or its free-space motion without knowing which robot it runs on.

10 Benchmarks and Tasks

This section gives the protocol that all simulation experiments share and then the setting of each benchmark and its tasks. The real-robot tasks are described in Section 14.

10.1 Sessions

Agents.

Every experiment is a session of one coding agent in its own command-line harness: Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 or, on four RoboDojo tasks and one BEHAVIOR-1K task, Codex with a GPT-6 model, at the xhigh reasoning effort unless stated otherwise. A session provides one or more simulated environments; with more than one, the agent may start subagents of the same model, which share its workspace and its budget. The weights of the model are never updated.

Workspace.

The agent starts from an empty workspace. Its folders for code, notes, and outputs are empty, and it holds only the instructions of the harness, the task description, the contract of the tool interface, and the skills of the platform, composed for the embodiment and the observation mode of the session (Section 9); the agent keeps no memory from earlier sessions. It runs in a container without network access, with 16 GB of memory and four CPUs, and reaches the simulator only through its tools. Every program it registers runs in a fresh container with 8 GB of memory, four CPUs, and no network access.

Task information.

The task description is generated from the public definition of the task; its content differs between benchmarks and is given below. Images of the completed task are frames of successful official demonstrations, either the final frame of each or a sequence of keyframes along each. They contain no actions and no states, and only the exploring agent sees them, never its programs. During an interactive episode, the agent may ask the benchmark’s evaluator whether the task is complete.

Budget and scenes.

The exploration budget counts exploration episodes. A single ledger charges every episode start and every rehearsal, across all environments and subagents, and the agent sees how many episodes remain. The budget is an upper bound, since submission ends exploration. Exploration scenes come in a fixed order, which the agent cannot choose, from the training distribution of the benchmark, and evaluation scenes from its official evaluation set, which exploration never uses.

Limits.

Each episode has the native step limit of the benchmark and a wall-clock limit, which during an interactive episode also bounds the agent’s own deliberation. The agent and its programs may call a vision-language model, Gemini 3.8 Flash, with a budget of $10 per session that exploration and evaluation share.

10.2 Rehearsal and Evaluation

Rehearsal.

When the agent considers its program ready, it freezes a copy of its code with a registered entry point into a bundle and requests a rehearsal. The bundle is executed alone in a fresh isolated environment on a new exploration scene while the agent is paused, and the rehearsal consumes one exploration episode, like an episode in which the agent acts itself. Afterwards, the agent reads the outcome and the logs of the rehearsal and may revise the bundle and rehearse again. Only a bundle that has completed a rehearsal without error can be submitted, and submission ends exploration.

Fully automated program.

Evaluation executes the submitted bundle on each unseen scene in a fresh isolated environment, without the agent and without edits or retries. The results are never revealed to the agent. Because the bundle calls the same tools that the agent called during exploration, the program that is evaluated is the program that was rehearsed.

Agent-in-the-loop program.

At the end of exploration, the workspace is frozen, including the code, the notes, the handoff, and a compressed version of the conversation. For each evaluation scene, a fresh copy of the agent starts from this frozen workspace and attempts the scene, running its code, observing, and acting through the same tools as during exploration.

Scoring.

Both forms are scored by the benchmark’s native evaluator, with partial credit wherever the benchmark defines it. An error, a timeout, or an early exit of the program counts as a failure, and scores are averaged over all scheduled evaluation episodes.

10.3 RoboDojo

Tasks and interface.

We use seven tasks of RoboDojo-Sim (Chen et al., 2026a) with the dual-arm ARX X5 (Table 13). The agent commands absolute joint targets at 25 Hz, six arm joints and a gripper opening for each arm, with between 1 and 50 rows per call. It may also command bounded end-effector steps, plan collision-free motions of one arm against the robot and the table, lift pixels to 3D points, and preview a motion on the robot alone. It observes the scene through a high camera and a camera on each wrist at 640×\times480; the benchmark renders RGB, and the harness adds metric depth, the intrinsics, and the pose of every camera.

Task information.

The task description is the public scoring rubric of the task, which for the randomized variants is that of the base task, with its score table. For make kong, pour by language, and swap blocks it adds a short clarification of the conditions, and for plug in charger and pour by language a summary of the official task code without its numeric thresholds. The agent also receives one image of the completed task, the last frame of the official video of the task.

Exploration and evaluation.

A single agent explores a single environment; on plug in charger and pour by language it may start one subagent. Exploration scenes are the layouts of one official collection in order, which repeat once the collection is exhausted, and the program is evaluated on the first layouts of another collection (Table 13); on hang mugs random, both come from a pooled collection, with evaluation on layouts 0 to 49 and exploration on layouts 50 to 89. An episode is limited to 6 s of wall-clock time per allowed step. A score is 100 on native success and the native partial score otherwise. The parallel experiment (Table 7) uses make toast with a description that includes the numeric thresholds, keyframes of a completed run, and 32 evaluation layouts from a third collection; the RGB-only sessions of Table 8 receive no depth, calibration, or pixel lifting.

10.4 BEHAVIOR-1K

Tasks and interface.

We use six tasks of the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge (Li et al., 2023) with the Galaxea R1Pro, in the official evaluation environment of BEHAVIOR-1K (Table 14). The agent commands the native action at 30 Hz, base velocity together with absolute joint targets of the four trunk joints and the two seven-joint arms and a command for each gripper, with between 1 and 150 rows per call. It may also move the base in closed loop, step an end effector through inverse kinematics, plan collision-free arm motions, lift pixels to 3D points, and preview a motion on the robot alone. It observes the scene through the head camera at 720×\times720 and a camera on each wrist at 480×\times480, all RGB-D with intrinsics and poses relative to the base, together with the official proprioception and an odometry estimate integrated from the base velocity. The step limit of an episode is 1.5 times the mean length of the human demonstrations of the task, as in the 2026 evaluation, whereas the 2025 challenge allowed twice the mean.

Task information.

The task description contains the official instruction, the goal and initial conditions of the task’s BDDL definition, the scene and its rooms, and the limits of an episode. Except on boxing books, the agent also receives keyframes of successful official demonstrations from the head camera: the first frame, the end of each annotated skill, the final frame, and enough frames in between that no gap exceeds 10 s.

Exploration and evaluation.

Exploration scenes are the 300 training instances of each task, and evaluation uses the test instances 301 to 310 (Table 14). An episode is limited to 900 s plus 0.5 s per allowed step. Boxing books is evaluated as a fully automated program and the other five tasks as agent-in-the-loop programs, with one fresh copy of the agent per test instance. On sorting items, clearing food, and clean up desk, each copy also receives the reports that a review model, Gemini 3.8 Flash, wrote on the fully automated program’s runs on the other nine test instances, built from the final status of each goal condition, the partial score, the program’s log, and camera frames, and referring to objects only by their task names. Episodes are scored by the Q-score of the challenge: 1 on success and otherwise the fraction of goal conditions that become satisfied during the episode, maximized over the alternative groundings of the goal and averaged over the ten instances.

10.5 HumanoidArena

Tasks and interface.

We use the seven tasks of HumanoidArena (Wang et al., 2026b) that have official test episodes, with a Unitree G1 that has 29 body joints and Dex3 hands (Table 15). The agent commands the official 40-dimensional whole-body reference at 50 Hz, with between 1 and 100 frames per call: the root translation and height, which the SONIC tracker (Luo et al., 2026) does not follow, since the robot translates only by stepping, the root orientation relative to the initial heading, 29 joint targets, and an open or close command for each hand. It may also plan collision-free motions of the arms, optionally with the waist, and lift pixels to 3D points in the pelvis frame and in a gravity-aligned frame. It observes the scene through the head camera at 640×\times480 in RGB-D, with the intrinsics and the camera pose in the pelvis frame, together with the root orientation, the joint positions and velocities, and the state of the hands. An episode ends when the robot falls, by the rule of the benchmark.

Task information.

The agent can read three teleoperated demonstrations of the task from the official raw dataset. Each is a complete episode with the 40-dimensional references, joint states, root poses, and the head camera’s RGB video and depth. The demonstrations are mounted read-only for the exploring agent only; its programs may contain motion segments that the agent cut from them (Section 11.3).

Exploration and evaluation.

We use Claude Opus 5.5 as our agent. Exploration scenes use seeds derived from a hash that excludes every official seed. Sessions with a budget above 32 explore two environments and may start two subagents. An episode is limited to 600 s plus 1 s per allowed step. The program is evaluated on the 60 official test episodes of each task, seeds 0, 1, and 2 with 20 episodes each, derived as in the official evaluation; every episode runs in a fresh simulator and container, four in parallel, and the simulator advances only when the program sends actions. Success is binary, and a fall or an error counts as a failure.

10.6 DexJoCo

Tasks and interface.

We use the eleven tasks of DexJoCo (Wang et al., 2026a) in its rand-obj setting, in which the placement of the objects and the height of the table are randomized at every reset (Table 16). Single-arm tasks use one Franka Panda arm with a 16-degree-of-freedom Allegro hand, and bimanual tasks use two. The agent commands the official policy action of the benchmark: for each arm, an absolute target for the flange position and orientation in the world frame, the orientation as a rotation vector, together with sixteen hand joint targets, which gives a 22-dimensional row for one arm and a 44-dimensional row for two. The official operational-space controller pulls the flange toward its target and position actuators drive the hand joints, without a motion planner. Each row advances the simulation by 20 ms, and one call to the interface executes between 1 and 150 rows. Observations are 640×\times640 RGB-D images from the official cameras of each task, with depth in millimeters and the intrinsics and world pose of every camera, together with the official proprioceptive state, the flange pose of each arm and the joint positions of each hand. No force, torque, contact, or tactile signal is exposed, and the object poses and table height in the simulator’s state never reach the agent. The interface also offers a dry run of a motion on the robot alone, without the table and objects, that does not advance the episode, and helpers for rotation arithmetic and for lifting a pixel with its depth to a world position.

Task information.

The agent receives a task description generated from the task definition: the official instruction, the robot and its cameras, the step limit and wall-clock limit of an episode, the fact that object placement and table height change between episodes, and the binary success criterion without partial credit. It contains no detail of the success check. The agent also receives three images of the completed task, the final frames of three successful human demonstrations from the official dataset, each in a different layout, taken from the task’s overview camera. They contain no actions and no states. The three demonstrations are the first that replay successfully in the official environment from initial layouts that differ from all 150 evaluation layouts.

Exploration.

A session gives one agent, Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at the xhigh effort setting and without subagents, one simulated environment, and a budget of N∈{2,4,8,16,32}N\in\{2,4,8,16,32\} exploration episodes. The agent starts from an empty workspace (Section 10.1). A exploration episode is either interactive, in which the agent drives the robot itself through the interface or through its own scripts, or a rehearsal, in which its registered program runs alone in a fresh container on a fresh episode while the agent is paused; both consume the budget. The agent ends exploration by submitting a program that has completed a rehearsal without error, so the budget is an upper bound, and over the 55 sessions the agents used 592 of the 682 budgeted episodes (Table 17). Exploration layout ii is the first reset of the official rand-obj environment with seed 1000+i1000+i, the same randomization as in evaluation, whose layouts come from seeds 0 to 2. An episode is limited to the official number of steps and to 600 s plus 5 s per allowed step of wall-clock time, a limit that no episode reached. The agent and its programs may call a vision-language model, Gemini 3.8 Flash, with a budget of $10 per session.

Evaluation.

Once the agent has exited, its workspace is frozen, and the submitted program is evaluated alone on 150 episodes that reproduce the official evaluation of DexJoCo layout for layout: seeds 0, 1, and 2, with 50 consecutive resets each. Every episode runs in a fresh simulator process and a fresh container for the program, four episodes in parallel, under the official step limit and success check, and an error or an early exit of the program counts as a failure. The simulator advances only when the program sends actions, so evaluation is synchronous and free of inference latency, whereas the official client of the benchmark is asynchronous.

10.7 LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro

Tasks and interface.

We use the 40 tasks of the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites of LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) in the official environment, numbered from 0 in the official order, and the position-perturbed variants of LIBERO-Pro (Zhou et al., 2025), in which objects exchange their initial regions. The agent commands the official action at 20 Hz, increments of the end-effector position and rotation, scaled so that 1 corresponds to 5 cm or 0.5 rad, and a gripper command, with between 1 and 100 rows per call and no motion planner. It observes the scene through the agent-view and wrist cameras at 256×\times256 in RGB-D, with the intrinsics and the pose of each camera, together with the end-effector pose and the finger positions, and it may lift pixels to 3D points. The step limit of an episode is 220 on Spatial, 280 on Object, 300 on Goal, and 520 on Long, after ten initial steps without motion.

Task information.

The task description contains the official instruction, the robot and its cameras, the limits of an episode, and the binary success criterion without the detail of its check. The agent also receives three images of the completed task, the final agent-view frames of three official human demonstrations that replay successfully.

Exploration and evaluation.

We use Claude Opus 5.5 as our agent in two environments. The budget is up to 20 exploration episodes on the official placement distribution, followed by at most 5 optional episodes of adaptation on the perturbed distribution, which the agent may use when it judges that its program will not transfer (Section 11.4). Exploration layout ii is a fresh reset of the official environment with seed 1000+i1000+i, a sample of the official placement distribution and never a stored initial state. An episode is limited to 600 s plus 5 s per allowed step. The program is evaluated on the 50 official initial states of each task and on the 50 position-perturbed states of LIBERO-Pro, each episode in a fresh container, synchronously, and with binary success. Adaptation episodes are fresh resets of the perturbed task with seeds from 2000.

11 Simulation Case Studies

This section follows single sessions on the simulation benchmarks in detail: what the agent explored, the program it wrote, and how that program behaves on unseen scenes.

11.1 Re-Perception Under Perturbation: Two Cans into a Basket

The first task of the LIBERO-Long suite asks the robot to put both the alphabet soup and the tomato sauce in the basket, on a table that also holds a ketchup bottle, a carton of orange juice, milk, butter, and cream cheese. The agent explored the task for 15 episodes in about an hour, ten of them interactive and five rehearsals of its program, and wrote a program of 1,362 lines that succeeds in all 50 official initial states and in 44 of the 50 perturbed states of LIBERO-Pro. The perturbation exchanges the soup with the ketchup and the tomato sauce with the orange juice, which moves the two cans by 15 and 32 cm (Figure 14a). This section shows what the program perceives, how it plans, and why its behavior transfers.

Perception.

The program perceives the scene anew in every round, and it divides the work between a vision-language model and depth (Figure 13). Gemini only names the objects: it returns a pixel on each can and in the basket, together with a short description of each can’s state. Every geometric quantity comes from depth. The program lifts the agent-view depth into the world frame, takes the table as the mode of the point heights, and, starting from each Gemini pixel, segments the object by a flood fill over 3D-connected points; the top height is a high percentile of the segment, and the axis is the centroid of its top 1.2 cm. A segment counts as a can only if its top is 4.5 to 8 cm wide and 5 to 30 cm above the table, bounds that the agent set after measuring every object on the table and that reject the taller and narrower ketchup bottle. A second detector, which uses depth alone, finds flat, round plateaus of the size of a lid and adds any can that Gemini missed. Before grasping, the program hovers 7 cm above the lid and refits the lid disk from the wrist camera; a top that is not can-shaped is blacklisted, and the grasp yaw is the first of four candidates whose finger zones are clear of other objects.

Placing by footprint reach.

The agent-view camera cannot see the floor of the basket, which its near wall hides, and the agent found during exploration that this flat floor is only about 7 by 10 cm: drop spots chosen by clearance put the second can’s footprint over the sloped walls, where the can stalled. The program therefore maps the interior from the wrist camera while it holds the first can, as a height map with 4 mm cells, and computes for every cell the highest point under the footprint of a can, its footprint reach (Figure 13c,d). It chooses the pair of spots, at least 6.8 cm apart, that minimizes the larger of their two reaches, releases each can just above its reach, and remaps the basket after the first release. During exploration, the agent also arranged perturbed layouts of its own, stacking the tomato sauce on the soup, standing the soup on the cream-cheese box, placing the cans side by side, and pushing the basket by 8 cm and rotating it by 20∘, and it ran its program on each of them.

Why the program transfers.

Nothing in the program refers to where the objects stood during exploration, so the perturbation changes its inputs but not its procedure. Under perturbation, its first estimate of each can’s axis lies within a median of 3.1 mm of the ground truth, against 2.9 mm on the official layouts, and the wrist refit within a median of 1.0 mm, while the cans themselves moved by 15 and 32 cm (Figure 14b); a policy that reproduced its official motions would miss each can by that displacement. The checks also absorb labelling errors. When Gemini placed the soup’s label on the ketchup bottle, which now stands where the soup stood in the official layouts, the wrist refit measured a top 3.7 cm across, and the program rejected it as not can-shaped, blacklisted its position, and found the soup in the next round. All six failures share one cause: the soup is not visible from the agent-view camera at the start, and the program, which re-perceives only from its home pose, stops with about 300 steps left. The listings below condense the program’s main loop and give the agent’s code for the footprint reach and the choice of drop spots, without docstrings and one log line.

{raxpseudo}

run(), condensed from controller.py def run(robot): table_z = mode of the agent-view point heights repeat up to 3 rounds: # perceive anew in every round lids = flat, round plateaus in depth # depth alone labels = Gemini(agent view) # one pixel per can and the basket cans = [flood_fill(p) for p in labels if is_can(top width, height)] cans += lids that no label explains, minus blacklisted positions for can in order(cans): # stacked cans: the higher first hover 7 cm above the lid; refit the lid disk from wrist depth if not can_shaped(disk): blacklist(can); continue yaw = first of 0, 90, 45, -45 deg with clear finger zones descend to top - 3 cm; close; lift if not 3.5 cm < finger opening < 7.4 cm: continue if no basket map: map the basket from the wrist, holding the can spot = plan_spots(map) for the first can, else lowest_spot(remap) lower to the release height above the footprint reach; open; lift if task complete: return

{raxcode}

[firstnumber=148]basket.py\raxcodesepfootprint reach and drop-spot planning def footprint_max(b, r=0.036): H = np.where(np.isfinite(b["H"]), b["H"], b["rim_z"]) # unobserved cells count as rim res = b["grid"][2] k = int(np.ceil(r / res)) yy, xx = np.mgrid[-k:k + 1, -k:k + 1] fp = (xx ** 2 + yy ** 2) * res ** 2 <= r * r # disk of the can’s footprint return ndimage.maximum_filter(H, footprint=fp, mode="constant", cval=b["rim_z"])

def plan_spots(b, r=0.036, min_sep=0.068): F = footprint_max(b, r) ii, jj = np.nonzero(b["interior"]) if len(ii) < 2: return None f = F[ii, jj] keep = np.argsort(f)[:400] ii, jj, f = ii[keep], jj[keep], f[keep] res = b["grid"][2] D = np.hypot(ii[:, None] - ii[None], jj[:, None] - jj[None]) * res cost = np.maximum(f[:, None], f[None]) + 0.5 * np.maximum(0.0, 0.08 - D) cost[D < min_sep] = np.inf a, c = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(cost), cost.shape) if not np.isfinite(cost[a, c]): return None s1, s2 = cell_xy(b["grid"], ii[a], jj[a]), cell_xy(b["grid"], ii[c], jj[c]) return [(s1, float(f[a])), (s2, float(f[c]))]

11.2 Self-Calibration and Grasp Design: Tower of Hanoi with Two Dexterous Hands

The bimanual Tower of Hanoi task of DexJoCo asks for the final two moves of a three-level tower: the medium red disk goes from the middle peg onto the large blue disk on the right peg, and the small yellow disk from the left peg on top of it. Two Franka arms carry 16-degree-of-freedom Allegro hands, and the disks slide over pegs that stand 13 cm above them, so a grasp has to hold a disk level as it travels along its peg without touching the peg. The agent received no grasp and no model of the hand, only the joint semantics and a few generic postures in its skills. It wrote a program that completed all 150 formal episodes on unseen layouts, in which the board shifts by up to 4.9 cm and the table height varies by as much.

Measuring its own fingertips.

The agent spent its first episode on its own hand, without touching a disk. It moved single joints of the right hand and lifted the wrist cameras’ depth into world points to see what each joint moves, finding that the first thumb joint turns the thumb from pointing sideways to pointing straight down and that the last two flex its tip forward. It then held the posture it meant to grasp with, the index finger and the thumb both pointing down, segmented the white fingertip caps in the right wrist camera, lifted them to 3D, and split them into two clusters (Figure 15). Relative to the measured flange, the thumb cluster lies at (−3.3,4.1,−15.7)(-3.3,4.1,-15.7) cm and the index cluster at (7.3,3.1,−12.9)(7.3,3.1,-12.9) cm; the agent adopted tip offsets of (−2.4,3.8,−16.3)(-2.4,3.8,-16.3) and (8.3,3.6,−13.3)(8.3,3.6,-13.3) cm, about 1 cm toward the centre of each tip, and every grasp of its program is built on them, as the first listing at the end of this section shows. The agent never saw a model of the hand, yet its thumb offset lies within 1.1 mm of the fingertip of the official model. Its index offset lies 27 mm from the model’s, because the camera sees only the upper part of that cap, but the error shifts the planned pinch line by only about 8 mm across a 7.7 cm disk. The same measurements placed the wrist camera at (−14.0,−3.0,4.1)(-14.0,-3.0,4.1) cm from the flange, exactly where the official model puts it.

Designing the grasp.

The agent then designed its grasp by trying candidates on the red and yellow disks (Figure 16). A palm-down hook pressed the palm onto the disk, and flexing the thumb turned the disk by 45∘ about its peg. A palm-down pinch at the wall of the disk lifted it, but the disk swung by about 40∘ about the pinch line, which the agent measured to pass 2.8 cm from the disk’s centre of mass, and a firmer squeeze dropped it. A side pinch lifted the yellow disk by 10 cm before it slipped back onto its peg, and a cage grasp left only 4 mm between the hand’s fixed thumb–index gap of 8.1 cm and the 7.7 cm red disk, so that only the thumb touched it. From these failures, the agent derived that rolling the hand by an angle θ\theta moves the index edge of the palm 0.10​sin⁡θ−0.013​cos⁡θ0.10\sin\theta-0.013\cos\theta m away from the thumb–index line, so that a roll of about 25∘ clears the peg and lets the pinch line pass through the centre of the disk. The resulting rolled vertical pinch, with a roll of 0.44 rad, held both disks through a 22 cm lift and a 40 cm carry in the fourth episode.

The program.

On every layout, the program measures the disks and pegs from the egocentric depth image, pinches both disks at once, and moves the red disk first while the left hand waits. It verifies every lift by measuring the held disk from three cameras, and it opens, backs off, and pinches again when the disk rose less than half of the lift. Because each arm keeps converging to its command after a move, the agent measured the tracking lag, which decays by a factor of 0.78 every five steps, and the program aligns the disk with the peg on its predicted final position rather than on its current one. Before submitting, the agent injected alignment errors of 8 and 15 mm and a missed pinch into its own runs, and the program recovered from all of them; its five versions completed all of their autonomous runs.

Precision on unseen layouts.

The program’s estimate of the target peg follows the hidden pose of the board across all 150 formal layouts, with residual standard deviations of 0.24, 0.05, and 0.18 mm in xx, yy, and height (Figure 17). After placing the red disk, the program measures its top again and finds it on average 0.66 mm, and at most 1.0 mm, below the height it predicted from the blue disk, the counterpart of the 6.5 mm check on the air fryer (Section 14.2.1).

{raxcode}

def pinch_pose(side, c, half, yaw, mid, gap_t=0.006, dz=-0.010): """Flange pose so thumb tip is gap_t outside the near face and the thumb-index line crosses the centre.""" c = np.asarray(c, float) th_off = world_offset(side, TH_TIP, ROLL, yaw) ix_off = world_offset(side, IX_TIP, ROLL, yaw) u = np.array([np.cos(yaw), np.sin(yaw)]); v = np.array([-np.sin(yaw), np.cos(yaw)]) lat_t = (th_off[:2] @ v - ix_off[:2] @ v) / 2 t_xy = c + (-half - R_T - gap_t) * u + lat_t * v t = np.array([t_xy[0], t_xy[1], mid + dz]) flange = t - th_off rv = rotvec_near(hand_rot(side, ROLL, yaw), np.array([-np.pi, 0, 0])) return flange, rv

{raxpseudo}

11.3 From Exploration to Code: Carrying a Hammer over a Bar on a Humanoid

In the DoubleDesk task of HumanoidArena, a Unitree G1 humanoid has to take a hammer from one desk, carry it over a bar on the floor, and drop it into a basket on a second desk. The agent commands the robot through whole-body kinematic references that a learned tracker, SONIC, executes; it was given the tracker, three teleoperated demonstrations, a forward-kinematic model of the robot, and a tool that returns the level frame of the pelvis. Over 125 exploration episodes and 10.7 hours, it wrote a program of 3,639 lines in eleven files, of which the 637-line kinematic model is the one it was given. The program completed 34 of the 60 formal episodes; before submitting it, the agent predicted “roughly half to two-thirds”.

Perception.

Every quantity the program uses comes from the depth image of the head camera, lifted into a point cloud in the level frame of the pelvis (Figure 18). The rotation into that frame comes from the provided tool, and the agent’s own fit of the floor plane by random sample consensus agrees with it to within 0.07∘. On this cloud, the agent’s code finds the floor as the mode of the point heights, the bar as the dominant line among points 5 to 11 cm above the floor, the desk tops and their near edges among upward-facing points, and the back wall, and it localizes the robot from the bar, the desks, and the wall against a map whose constants it measured itself. It finds the hammer by its orange handle, takes the handle’s principal axis, decides which end carries the head from the dark points beyond the handle, and measures its length, using the 0.302 to 0.310 m it found during exploration to place the centre when part of the hammer is hidden; on the unseen scene of Figure 18, the length is 0.305 m. It finds the basket as the largest cluster of points above a desk and fits a rectangle of 0.60 by 0.40 m with its rim 0.90 m above the floor, and it measures the distance of each sole from the bar by combining the fitted bar with the kinematic model. The program perceives anew at every stage and before every step at the bar, and after a grasp it confirms that the hammer is held by measuring the height of the handle again.

Locomotion and the bar.

The agent’s skills recommended walking by replaying a cycle cut from a teleoperated recording. The agent cut a symmetric 66-step cycle from one demonstration, looped it with a ramp in heading, and measured that its amplitude does not control the length of a single step, which varied by ±\pm10 cm; it therefore calibrated multi-step walks against its own localization and used them as a table of distances. Sidestepping moved the robot by 1 to 2 cm per cycle, so lateral placement turns and then walks. The crossing replays the step over the bar from one demonstration: with the recorded pitch, the pelvis did not travel and the lead foot landed on the bar, so the agent scaled the pitch to zero; perpendicular approaches landed the lead foot on the edge of the bar, so it approaches at 64∘, where the swinging foot also reaches sideways; and it adds a trailing step when the robot ends astride the bar, after learning never to turn in that position. Whether a crossing succeeds depends on the stance from which it starts, and the agent built a model of how each step moves the two soles relative to the bar, from its own measurements of 102 transitions (Figure 19a). The model predicts that a left step places the left sole 14.5 cm ahead of the right one up to an amplitude of 0.35, and up to 25 cm at 0.6; a planner searches three actions ahead to bring the left sole into the window from which the program crosses. The bounds of that window are measured too: crossings started with the left sole within 21 cm of the bar succeeded in 17 of 17 trials, which set the far edge of the window at 21.5 cm, and the trailing sole is kept within 37 cm of it, since the agent found that crossings with the trailing sole closer than 35.5 cm had succeeded 27 times out of 27, and those with it between 35.5 and 42 cm had fallen 4 times out of 13. The agent then wrote its own Monte Carlo simulators of the approach, which replay the stance model with its measured errors, and used them to choose that margin, which lowered the simulated risk of a fall from 9.3 to about 6% at a cost of 0.3 actions. Over all 137 crossings in its logs, every crossing started with the trailing sole within 35.5 cm of the bar succeeded, and in the formal evaluation the robot crossed the bar in all 59 logged episodes without a fall (Figure 19b). In the episode of Figure 18c, the model predicted that the left step would bring the left sole to 16.7 cm before the bar, and the point cloud measured it at 17.3 cm.

The program and its versions.

The program runs seven stages, each with its own checks: it approaches the hammer until the handle lies at about 60∘ to its heading, which the agent found to give grasps that hold; it grasps with up to two attempts, treating a closure without torque as a miss; it carries the hammer to the bar while correcting its odometry from the bar and the basket; it plans its stance at the bar and crosses only from the window; it verifies after the crossing that both soles are past the bar; and it finds the basket and places the hammer inside its fitted rectangle. Each stage has a deadline in steps, measured from the durations of earlier runs. The agent kept its own table of every stage in every episode, linked each failure to the change it made, and grew the program over more than thirty versions (Tables 18 and 20). Its interactive and rehearsal runs completed 41 of 82 episodes, rising to 6 of 9 for the final versions, and in the formal evaluation most failures occurred at the grasp, which held in 40 of the 59 logged episodes.

11.4 Adaptation Under Perturbation on LIBERO-Pro

After its exploration on unperturbed layouts, RAX may adapt its program to the perturbed distribution of LIBERO-Pro. A subagent reads the program, the description of the perturbed task, and the first frame of a perturbed layout, and judges whether the program will transfer. When it judges that the program will not, the agent resumes from its workspace, with the notes and code of its exploration, and continues for at most 5 episodes on perturbed layouts before the program is evaluated again on its own. In this mode, RAX runs as an agent-in-the-loop program across the change of distribution: the program acts alone, and the agent steps in only to revise it, so that adaptation exercises the continual learning of Section 3.4. The agent adapted its program on five of the 40 tasks, tasks 3, 8, and 9 of the Long suite and tasks 1 and 5 of the Goal suite (Table 19).

A mirrored cabinet.

The third task of the Long suite asks the robot to put the black bowl in the bottom drawer of the cabinet and close it. The program solved all 50 official states, but LIBERO-Pro places the cabinet on the other side of the table, facing the other way (Figure 21a,b), and the program, whose code assumed a drawer that opens toward −y-y, failed in all 50 perturbed states. Its checks kept it from acting blindly: in 38 of them, it found no drawer panel where it expected one and stopped at the first step. Resuming from its workspace, the agent identified the cause in its first episode on the perturbed layouts and, rather than rewriting the program, added a 36-line layer that mirrors the frame in which it plans: points, orientations, and action rows are reflected across the plane y=0y=0 whenever the cabinet stands at −y-y (the listing below). The program decides the side itself, from the flat top of the cabinet in the agent-view point cloud (Figure 21c). In a stress test, the agent moved the wine bottle in front of the drawer and found that its detector of the drawer panel took the bottle for the panel; it narrowed the detector’s window, and with its five episodes spent, the adapted program completed all 50 perturbed states (Figure 21d).

12 Exploration Budget of ASPIRE on LIBERO-Pro

ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) writes robot programs in CaP-X (Fu et al., 2026) with Claude Code and Claude Opus 4.6. Its programs call the CaP-X interfaces for perception, including text-prompted segmentation and vision-language pointing, for grasp planning, including a top-down grasp selector, for inverse kinematics, and for joint-space motion, and they may not read the simulator’s ground-truth state. On LIBERO-Pro, the unit of development is a task under one perturbation: each of the 30 tasks of the Spatial, Object, and Goal suites is developed separately for the position and the task perturbation, giving 60 programs, each written for its own perturbed suite.

For each task and perturbation, ASPIRE executes an initial program on a debugging split of 15 environment seeds (51–65), where a seed fixes one instance of the task, including object poses, distractors, and the initial state of the robot. After each execution, the coding agent reads a trace of every primitive call, with its inputs, outputs, and return status, the camera frames before and after the call, grasp candidates, object poses, and motion-planning results. It diagnoses the failure, patches the program, and replays the debugging seeds, with at most three replays per seed. On some tasks, an evolutionary search additionally proposes KK candidate programs per iteration, conditioned on the three best programs and their failure traces, and executes each candidate on the debugging split; the reported searches run for up to four iterations, and KK is not reported. The final program is executed once on a validation split of 15 further seeds (66–80) and then evaluated on seeds 1–50. A coordinator promotes validated repairs into a shared library of skills, each stored with its failure signature, its condition of use, its repair strategy, and a code sketch, which later sessions read as in-context guidance. With the same loop on Claude Opus 5, Kang et al. (2026) report a median of 0.99 hours and 91 thousand output tokens per task and perturbation.

The debugging and validation seeds index instances of the same perturbed suite as the evaluation seeds, so every rollout before the final evaluation is drawn from the distribution on which the program is evaluated. This is also required by the task perturbation, which changes the goal of the task: a program developed on the original task would pursue the original goal. ASPIRE’s result on the Long suite comes from a separate setting, in which a skill library built on the 90 tasks of LIBERO-90 is applied to the Long tasks without any debugging on them. ASPIRE does not report the total number of rollouts per task; Table 20 gives the budget that its protocol implies, alongside that of RAX. With at most 5 rollouts from the evaluation distribution on the five tasks that adapted to the perturbation (Section 11.4), and none on the other 35, RAX exceeds ASPIRE on every suite under position perturbation, by 28.2 points on Spatial, 2.0 on Object, 6.0 on Goal, and 48.8 on Long (Table 6).

13 Summary Results of 1

The two simulation charts of 1 summarize RoboDojo, BEHAVIOR-1K, HumanoidArena, DexJoCo, and LIBERO-Pro, and compare RAX with the strongest prior model, that is, with learned policies such as VLAs and world action models rather than with other agents. For each benchmark, the right chart pairs the average success rate of RAX, with each task at its largest budget, with the average of the strongest prior model on the same tasks: VPP2 on RoboDojo, the highest-ranked challenge entry on BEHAVIOR-1K, WB-WAM on HumanoidArena, ME-Dex on DexJoCo, and VPP2 on LIBERO-Pro. On LIBERO-Pro, the chart therefore compares with VPP2 (42.3%), the strongest model under position perturbation, and not with the coding agent ASPIRE (63.2%), which we compare with in Section 5.2.5. On DexJoCo, the chart includes only the five bimanual tasks, iPad, Hanoi, Assembly, Microwave, and Photo. The six single-arm tasks are too easy to show the effect of scaling, since RAX solves each of them within a few exploration episodes, and the bimanual tasks are the harder part of the benchmark: with 32 exploration episodes, RAX averages 94.3% on them, against 48.8% for ME-Dex. The average margin of 37.4 points stated in the abstract and the introduction is the mean of the five margins of this chart, 53.4 on RoboDojo, 38.3 on BEHAVIOR-1K, 7.9 on HumanoidArena, 45.5 on the bimanual tasks of DexJoCo, and 42.1 on LIBERO-Pro.

The per-benchmark margins listed in the introduction instead compare with the strongest prior result of any kind on all tasks of each benchmark. On DexJoCo, this is the average of all eleven tasks at 32 exploration episodes, 96.7%, against ME-Dex at 65.3% (+31.4), and on LIBERO-Pro it is ASPIRE (+21.2). Section 5.2.4 further reports the best session of each task across budgets, which averages 99.5%. The left chart averages, at each budget, the success rates of the tasks within each benchmark and then the five benchmarks with equal weight. A task without a result at a budget shown counts with its result at the largest smaller budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 37 of the 40 tasks have a budget of 15 exploration episodes and use 11 to 15, Goal 1, 5, and 9 have a budget of 20 and use 18, 20, and 19, and the 40 tasks use 14.2 on average (13.5 on Spatial, 14.0 on Object, 15.1 on Goal, and 14.0 on Long), so their results are included at 16. The dashed line, 41.2%, is the mean of the strongest prior models of the right chart.

14 Real-Robot Tasks

This section describes the setup of every real-robot experiment: the task, the robot and its sensors, what the agent was given, what the operator did, how many trials the agent ran, how success was judged, and the final outcome. Five tasks use a Franka FR3 arm with a parallel gripper, two exterior RGB-D cameras (left and right of the table), and an RGB-D camera on the wrist; the sixth uses a Rainbow RB-Y1 mobile manipulator with an RGB-D camera on its head. The control interfaces are those of Section 4.2. In every task the agent received only the task text quoted below, typed by the operator, and the robot’s tools; it received no demonstrations, no object models, and no trained policy. Each session ran Claude Code with maximum reasoning effort. The agent could send requests to the operator through its tools, and the operator could reply in a chat; we report every reset and intervention recorded in the agent’s notes. Times are local wall-clock times taken from the agent’s notes and the camera recordings, which are timestamped frame by frame. The key-frame figures show raw camera frames without overlays.

14.1 Find the Cube

Task.

The operator hides a white cube of about 3 cm under one of four inverted green cups (about 9.3 cm tall) and shuffles the cups by hand; the robot must then lift the cup that holds the cube away and grasp and lift the cube. The task text was: “First wait for the operator to place a cube under a green cup and watch it permute the positions of the cups. after it finishes, you should identify the cup with the cube insides and lift the cup away, then grasp the cube and lift it in the gripper, as success.” The agent had to watch the shuffle while it happened: it held the arm still at a watch pose above the cups and recorded the wrist camera’s stream, then identified the cup from that recording.

Operator.

The operator hid the cube, shuffled the cups, and reset the scene between trials when the agent asked. During the session the operator made the game harder in three steps. At first the cube was covered by a cup and the cups were slid around. In later trials the operator also lifted the cube and moved it, or set a decoy cup on its old spot. From 21:35 the operator dropped the cube into an upright cup, not necessarily the nearest, turned that cup over, and then shuffled. From 21:50 the cube was replaced by a red wedge of about 4 cm.

Trials and outcome.

The agent ran 12 trials between 20:08 and 22:35, and recorded each in its notes; trials that stopped partway were resumed from the step that failed. In the first trial the shuffle started before the arm reached the watch pose. In the next two the agent finished parts by hand-issued commands, and in the third its tracker assumed a static cube and chose the decoy. Trials 4, 5, and 6 were three consecutive end-to-end successes of the agent’s program without intervention, in 166, 231, and 194 s. Trial 7 missed the moment the cup covered the cube; trial 8 identified the cup correctly but pinched the cube through the cup wall and carried both, after which the agent grasped cups higher and with less force. Trial 9 introduced a new way of hiding the cube: dropped into an upright cup that was then turned over. The program recognized no hiding event it knew and stopped without moving the robot. The agent adapted on the spot: it added a detector for a cube lying inside an upright cup, checked it on the recorded stream and on all seven recordings so far, and resumed the same scene one minute later, when the robot lifted the predicted cup and grasped the cube in 98 s (Figure 22). Figure 24 shows how its program tracks the cups. With the red wedge, the cup was identified correctly in trials 10 and 11; the wedge was grasped after several fixes and manual help in trial 10, and on the first attempt in the resumed trial 11 (Figure 23). For the wedge the agent kept the cup tracker and 20 of the program’s 41 functions unchanged, generalized its model of the hidden object to a measured size, color, and height, and changed the grasp to close on the wedge along two axes. Success was judged from the gripper width after the grasp and from the wrist camera’s view of the object in the gripper.

14.2 Air Fryer

Task.

The robot must open the drawer of an air fryer by its handle, put a banana into the basket, and close the drawer. The task text was: “You should open the air fry pan, put the banana inside, and close it. Reminder: the plate is really heavy and you should figure out where to grasp and the force applied. Also if the position of the air fry pan is out of range you may ask for operator reset. Be careful about the forces and maybe not pull out the plate entirely so we do not have to lift it in everytime.” The agent’s perception, its articulated model of the fryer, and its verification are described in Section 14.2.1.

Operator.

The operator reset the scene between runs; after the first run, for example, the operator took the banana out of the basket, which the robot cannot reach into. Between runs the fryer was moved (by about 6 cm and 4 cm in the two table directions before run 7) and rotated it (so that the handle faced the robot’s base, before run 8). Before the final run the operator moved the banana away from the left camera at the agent’s request and added an orange ball as a second object.

Runs and outcome.

The session lasted from 09:18 to 12:05. The agent first completed the task once by direct tool calls (run 1, about 75 minutes including exploration), then wrote a program and ran it nine times (runs 2–10). Run 2 ended with a safety stop when the elbow hit the left camera; the collision moved the right camera, which the agent stopped using. Runs 4, 5, and 8 needed resumes after a false-negative check, a descent timeout, and refused long moves, and run 8 also needed recovery commands issued by the agent. Runs 6, 7, 9, and 10 were clean unattended successes, including run 7 on the moved fryer and run 9 on the rotated one. In the final run the program opened the drawer by 13.1 cm, placed the banana and then the ball in the basket, and closed the drawer, in 210 s, leaving the handle 3.5 mm from its initial position; Figure 27 shows it. Figure 25 shows how its program handles the fryer’s layout, the camera bump, and the release. Success was judged by the agent’s own measurements: the drawer opening, the objects’ points inside the basket rim, and the handle’s final position.

14.2.1 Agent-Written 3D Perception

This section details the perception code behind Figure 3. The task is to open the drawer of an air fryer by its handle, put a banana into the basket, and close the drawer, on a real Franka FR3 with a left exterior and a wrist RGB-D camera. The agent wrote the perception and the program itself, in about 1,500 lines of Python; they use no learned detector and no vision-language model. All numbers below are from the agent’s final run.

Lifting to a metric frame.

Every depth pixel is back-projected with the camera intrinsics and the camera-to-base pose into the robot’s base frame, and the views of the exterior and wrist cameras are fused in that frame. All later computations operate on these points; estimates are projected back into the images only to check them.

Segmentation and geometric primitives.

Each part of the scene is selected by a colour threshold combined with a height band and a workspace region: the dark lid on top of the fryer, its white body, the dark handle outside the body, the yellow banana, and an orange ball just above the table. Geometric primitives are then fitted to the selected points, each with a plausibility check on its size:

  • •

    the fryer body, by a robust circle fit to its side (radius 8 to 16 cm accepted), and the lid, seen from the wrist camera above, by a second circle (4.5 to 8 cm), whose centre gives the fryer’s vertical axis cc;

  • •

    the handle, by the direction from the axis to its horizontal arm, which gives the pull direction dd, the outer face of its grip in 1.5 cm height slices, the height of its arm, and its lateral offset;

  • •

    the banana, by its principal axis and a quadratic centre line, which give its arc middle, the normal on its convex side, its chord (13 to 21 cm accepted; 18.0 cm here), and its height;

  • •

    the basket, once the drawer is open, by a circle fitted to its rim.

The pull direction from the top view must agree with the one from the side view within 12∘; the side view alone was biased by about 4∘4^{\circ}, which is why the agent added the top view.

Task frame and articulated model.

All targets are expressed in a frame anchored on the fryer: the axis cc, the pull direction dd, and t=z×dt=z\times d. The agent also wrote an articulated model of the fryer: a fixed upper cylinder and the back of the lower body, and a drawer cylinder with box models of the handle’s grip and arm, which translate together by the drawer’s opening along dd. The model provides a signed distance from any point, and the program instantiates it at the drawer’s current opening to check every planned motion for clearance between the arm, hand, fingers, wrist camera, and held object, and the fryer, the table, and keep-out regions around the exterior cameras.

How the agent built the model.

No model of the fryer was provided. The agent first completed the task once by hand, controlling the robot step by step, and recorded what it measured in its notes: the fryer’s top at a height of 0.415 m and the seam between body and drawer at 0.245 m, a handle with a horizontal arm and a hanging grip, and the basket centre relative to the handle once the drawer was out. It also noted that the drawer slides freely along the pull direction and tips slightly when released. About 90 minutes into the session it turned these observations into the model above, in the first version of its program, and revised it in later versions. Table 21 separates what the agent estimates in each new scene from what it fixed from these measurements.

Estimators.

The agent does not register the whole model to the point cloud at once. Instead, each parameter of the model comes from a small, robust estimate on the points of one part of the scene, illustrated on its final run in Figure 26:

  1. 1.

    Axis cc (Figure 26a). From the wrist camera above the fryer, the dark points at the height of the lid are fitted with a circle by least squares: writing the circle as x2+y2=2​a​x+2​b​y+kx^{2}+y^{2}=2ax+2by+k turns the fit into a linear system for the centre (a,b)(a,b) and kk, with radius k+a2+b2\sqrt{k+a^{2}+b^{2}}. The fit is repeated six times, each time discarding the points that lie farthest from the current circle, so that the dark inner part of the lid and stray points do not pull the centre away. The centre is the fryer’s axis; the radius, 6.3 cm here, must lie between 4.5 and 8 cm.

  2. 2.

    Pull direction dd (Figure 26b). Dark points at the height of the handle and just outside the lid are the handle’s arm seen from above. Points more than 0.25 rad from their median bearing around the axis are dropped, and dd points from the axis to the median of the rest; a median ignores the few points of other dark objects.

  3. 3.

    Handle face and arm height (Figure 26c). In the plane through the axis along dd, the handle’s points are cut into 1.5 cm height slices. In each slice, the 97th percentile of the distance along dd marks the handle’s outer face, the surface the fingers and the closing push rest on, while ignoring a few noisy points beyond it; the 95th percentile of height gives the top of the arm, which sets the grasp height.

  4. 4.

    Banana (Figure 26d). The banana’s yellow points are expressed along their principal axis, found by singular value decomposition, and a quadratic curve fitted by least squares gives its centre line. The middle of that curve is the grasp point, its bulge gives the convex side that sets the hand’s orientation, and its ends give the chord, 18.0 cm here, which must lie between 13 and 21 cm.

  5. 5.

    Basket rim (Figure 26e). After opening, the dark rim points are searched for around the rim predicted by the model and fitted with a circle in the same way as the lid. The measured centre lies 6.5 mm from the prediction, and the release poses use it.

The drawer’s opening is the shift of the handle face between the measurements before and after the pull, and the camera pose after the bump is a rigid transform fitted by least squares to feature matches that agree with each other within 8 mm.

Planning on the model.

Figure 27 shows each planned action on the real robot, numbered as in Figure 3(b). The handle grasp lies 1.2 cm inside the measured grip face along dd and 9 mm below the top of the arm, with the hand tilted 5∘5^{\circ} toward the fryer. The drawer is pulled 12.5 cm along dd in absolute 3 cm steps at a fixed height, since relative steps sagged under the drawer’s weight. The basket centre is predicted from the handle face and the opening, with an offset measured in the first manual run; the banana is released with its middle 1.5 cm beyond the basket centre and the hand tilted 60∘60^{\circ} about the banana’s axis, and the ball slightly further along dd. The drawer is closed by pushing along −d-d, finishing with the fingertips on the grip face.

Verification.

Each step is checked by a new measurement. The opening is the shift of the handle face (13.1 cm here), and the step fails if it falls more than 3 cm short of the command. The rim is searched for around the model’s prediction and found 6.5 mm from it, and the release poses use the measured rim. The banana counts as placed when its points lie inside the rim and below its height: 99.99% of them, with its top at 17.9 cm against a rim at 23.5 cm. Before closing, the handle is measured again, since the released drawer tips by about 2.5 cm and shifts sideways by about 1.5 cm; after closing, its face lies 3.5 mm from its initial position.

Sensor limits and calibration.

The agent recorded two limits of its sensors and coded around them: the wrist camera’s depth is unreliable closer than about 30 cm, so metric targets come from the exterior camera; and side-view pixels on the edge of the banana take the depth of the rim behind it, so heights are measured from the top-down wrist view. When the arm bumped the left camera, whose reported pose stayed unchanged, the agent re-estimated that pose by matching image features against frames captured before the bump, lifting the matches to 3D with both depth maps, and fitting a rigid transform, with a residual of 3.5 mm and fixed landmarks within 2 to 9 mm of their references. It applies the correction only to frames captured after the bump, and it stopped using the right camera, which had moved too far to correct.

14.3 Wiping a Stain

Task.

The robot must grasp a wet towel and wipe a soy-sauce stain off the table. The task text was: “You are given a wet towel, and I will ask you to wipe the soy sauce stain on the table using it. First get familiar with the robot and environment. When you are ready, please call for operator to pour the soy sauce on the table for you to wipe. Also, if you need help such as adding some soap to the towel also ask for operator help.” The towel is deformable and has no fixed shape on the table. The agent did not use force sensing: it pressed the towel onto the table by commanding a height 12 mm below the contact height it had measured.

Operator.

The operator poured soy sauce when the agent asked, washed the towel and added soap to it between trials, and returned it to the table as a loose heap. The stains differed from trial to trial in size (the agent measured 10 to 311 cm2), shape, and position, including one next to the left camera at the edge of the reachable workspace.

Trials and outcome.

The session lasted from 09:21 to 12:46. The agent first wiped a stain by direct tool calls (two passes; the first left a smeared film, and the second, after the operator added soap, cleaned it), then wrote a program that locates the towel heap, grasps a wad of it, locates the stain against a clean reference image, scrubs it in a back-and-forth pattern, parks the towel, and checks for residue. It ran the program in 13 recorded trials and resumes (trials 1 to 7b). Failures were a refused far reach, an operator reply the program did not expect, one false “clean” verdict on thin streaks (the operator asked for a second wipe; the agent then added a check with the wrist camera at 1 mm resolution), stains next to the left camera that required fitting the wiping region to the reachable area, and a refused approach move. The last two trials, 6 and 7b, cleaned the stain in one pass without intervention; trial 7b reused the scene of trial 7 after the agent fixed the approach move (Figure 28). Figure 30 shows how its program finds, wipes, and checks the stain. Success was judged by the agent’s residue measurement against the clean reference in the exterior and wrist cameras (0 cm2 in both for trials 6 and 7b) and by eye in the three camera views.

Adaptation to paper towels.

Afterwards the operator asked for a variant: “pull paper towels out of the box, wipe table, and then throw them into the waste bin.” The agent wrote a new program that imports the towel program unchanged and calls its parts: locating the stain against the clean reference, fitting the wiping region to the reachable area, the press-then-grasp of a wad, the zig-zag wipe 12 mm below the measured contact, and the residue check. The new code handles the paper: it finds the box and the bin, pinches the top of a protruding sheet and pulls it out, piles six sheets on the stain, releases the wad over the bin and scrapes paper stuck to the fingers, and sweeps up sheets left on the table. After three dry runs, the stain was removed in both wet runs (Figure 29), but leftover sheets, and in the second run a flat wet scrap that the sweep missed, were cleaned up with supervised scripts.

14.4 Peg Insertion: the ManipulationNet Peg-in-Hole Challenge

Task.

This is the peg-in-hole challenge of ManipulationNet (Chen et al., 2026b). Its board is a transparent acrylic plate of 320×250×25320\times 250\times 25 mm with blind holes 21.8 mm deep for five peg shapes, each at four clearance levels, rows L1 to L4 with 3, 1, 0.1, and 0.02 mm clearance. Neither the steel pegs, 50 mm long, nor the holes are chamfered. We used three pegs, the rectangle, the triangle, and the hexagon. The task text was: “There is a white transparent board in front and below you. There are openings on top that match the shape of the silver metal pegs (3 of them. rectangle. triangle and hexagon). You need to grasp them up and insert into the holes upright. Reminder: the depth of the wrist is not accurate at close distance, so you can locate approximately and probe the position and yaw based on force feedback, to succeed in the fine insertion. If you need help or if the position is of bad IK you can ask for operator to move it.” The agent converted the public CAD files of the board and the pegs into a model of the hole positions, which it registered to the wrist camera’s image. During the session the user asked it to work toward the tighter rows, from L2 to L3. L4 was not attempted.

Operator.

The board rests on the table unfixed. After the agent dragged it while lifting a jammed peg with a closed gripper, the operator taped the board to the table (at 01:30). The operator re-seated a hexagon peg that had toppled in L2 after a failed L3 attempt. The L3 fits are tight enough that the robot could not pull a seated peg out (15 N with rocking); before the final run the operator pulled the three pegs out of L3 and stood them upright on the table. The user also gave advice in the chat, for example to lower the peg further before turning it upright.

Exploration and outcome.

The agent worked by direct tool calls and its own scripts, supervised by the user; it never ran an unattended program in this task. Between 23:13 and 01:46 it inserted each peg into L1, L2, and L3 in turn (the triangle and the hexagon each failed once in L3 before succeeding). The user then asked for a full run, and between 02:28 and 03:22 the agent took each peg from the table and inserted it into L1, then L2, then L3, showing it upright in each row (Figure 31). Figure 32 shows how it registers the board, finds the holes by touch, and tilts the peg in. L3 needed a tilted entry with a corner of the peg first, followed by small rocking pushes while the peg was turned upright. All three pegs were seated in L3 at the end, at depths of 20.8 mm (hexagon), 19.7 mm (triangle), and 21.0 mm (rectangle), out of 21.8 mm. The full run took about 55 minutes including the operator’s extraction of the pegs from the earlier L3 attempts. Success was judged by the insertion depth the agent measured with the arm and by images of the upright pegs.

14.5 Bandu Tower

Task.

Bandu is a stacking game with irregular wooden pieces. The task text was a single sentence: “Stack the bandu blocks as the demonstrated tower.” The “demonstration” was a tower standing on the table when the session began; the agent was not shown how it was built. The tower stands on a base of four rectangular blocks laid in a 2×22\times 2 pattern and consists of seven pieces: a ring with a dowel standing in it, a barrel, a goblet with an urn seated in its cup and a knob seated in the urn, and an oblique cylinder that the user added at 13:42, asking for it on top of the barrel. Several of these placements leave little play, and the knob’s opening clearance was about 1 mm by the agent’s estimate. The user told the agent to take the tower apart and rebuild it, and to repair its own disturbances rather than rely on human resets.

Operator.

The operator reset the pieces once after the robot’s hand swept the tower (at 15:06, during a sideways pick the user had asked for), restarted or re-homed the gripper twice, and moved one piece the arm could not reach. The user asked for visual alignment instead of a contact search for the knob (“align with at most 1 mm opening error”).

Exploration and outcome.

The session lasted from 11:13 to 17:20. The agent first took the tower apart and rebuilt it by direct tool calls, then wrote a program with a disassembly and an assembly mode and alternated them over runs 1 to 15, fixing a failure after each stop. In the final exploration cycle the program disassembled the tower (7/7 pieces, 459 s) and then rebuilt it fully automatically, without intervention: 7/7 pieces in 663 s, the knob placed by visual alignment from both exterior cameras to an offset of 0.19 mm before insertion (Figure 33). Figure 34 shows how its program perceives, places, and checks each piece. Each placement was checked by the measured seat height and, for the urn, an uprightness check in both cameras; the final tower was compared with the demonstrated one in both exterior views.

14.6 Long-Horizon Tidying on the RB-Y1

Task.

The RB-Y1 must tidy a lab corner in six chained subtasks given in one instruction: “I want you to complete a series of tasks and you should reuse the skills while still monitor and control the process. First, you should move the chair in front of you out and park it to the left of the yellow table in front of you to clear it out of the way. then you should stack the two silver cups together and carry the stacked cups and banana over to the orange basket to your right and place them in, and pick up the orange basket on to the cabinet with dark top. Then you should move the chair back and tuck it to the table again. Finally you should pick up the box on your right and put it also on the cabinet. Be agile and reactive.” The robot perceives the scene only through its head camera and must move between the table, the basket, and the cabinet with its base.

Skills from earlier sessions.

The agent started from a shared skill library written in five earlier RB-Y1 sessions: carrying a box between the floor and a table (bimanual-box-pnp, from three sessions), lifting the basket onto the cabinet by its rim with both grippers (bimanual-bucket-rim-pnp), and moving and tucking an office chair (office-chair-tuck) and nesting two cups (stack-cups), both from one chair session. Carrying the cups and the banana into the basket had no skill. During the session the agent added a skill for reaching hand moves (oc-hand-reach) and a composition skill for the whole task, and updated the library after each trial.

Operator.

The operator reset the scene before each trial, stayed in the loop throughout, and gave advice in the chat, such as “straighten the arms”, “lift first”, and “check the torso and height against previous skills”. In trial 1 the robot’s base hit the cabinet during a hand-planned turn, after which the agent checked the base’s swept footprint before every base move. In trial 3 the operator re-armed the robot after controller faults while the cups were being nested.

Trials and outcome.

The agent ran the whole sequence three times; all six subtasks were completed in each trial (trials 1 and 2 overnight on the first day, trial 3 on the next evening). Trial 3, shown in Figure 5, ran from 19:31 to 21:09 (98 minutes), with the agent at every checkpoint of the skills. Success of each subtask was judged by the agent from head-camera images (for example, two rims visible for nested cups, both objects inside the basket, the basket and the box on the cabinet).

15 Compute and Cost

Across all experiments in this paper, simulated and real, the agents’ model calls consumed over 100k US dollars of API credits.
